sections.title: Nature, Definition and Essentials of Tort; Tort vs Contract and Crime
sections.summary: Foundation questions: definition, damnum sine injuria and injuria sine damno, mental element, maxims. Usually 1 question.
key_points: Indian tort law is largely UNCODIFIED judge-made law, built on English common law as adapted to Indian conditions (Art 372 continues pre-constitutional law; Indian courts apply 'justice, equity and good conscience'). Statutory supplements: Fatal Accidents Act 1855, Motor Vehicles Act 1988, Consumer Protection Act 2019, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991, National Green Tribunal Act 2010, Workmen's/ Employees' Compensation Act 1923.

Definition (Winfield): tortious liability arises from the breach of a duty primarily fixed by law; this duty is towards persons generally and its breach is redressible by an action for unliquidated damages. (Salmond: a civil wrong for which the remedy is a common law action for unliquidated damages and which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or breach of trust or other merely equitable obligation.) Tort = Latin 'tortum' (twisted/wrong).

Essentials: (1) a wrongful act or omission by the defendant; (2) the act must give rise to a legal duty (duty fixed by law, owed to the world at large); (3) the act must cause legal damage (violation of a legal right) - or be actionable per se; (4) the remedy is unliquidated damages (plus injunction etc.).

INJURIA SINE DAMNO: violation of a legal right without actual loss - actionable per se (trespass, libel, assault, battery, false imprisonment). Ashby v White (1703): a returning officer wrongly refused to register a qualified voter; the voter's right was violated though his candidate won - he was entitled to damages. DAMNUM SINE INJURIA: actual loss without violation of a legal right - not actionable. Gloucester Grammar School Case (1410): a schoolmaster could not sue for loss caused by a rival school; Mogul Steamship v McGregor Gow (1892): lawful competition; Bradford Corporation v Pickles (1895): an act lawful in itself is not made unlawful by a bad motive (but motive can matter in nuisance - Christie v Davey; Hollywood Silver Fox Farm v Emmett).

Tort vs CRIME: tort - private wrong, plaintiff sues for compensation, no fixed penalty; crime - wrong against society, prosecuted by State, punishment. Same act may be both (assault, defamation, negligence causing death, nuisance). TORT vs CONTRACT: duty fixed by law vs by parties' consent; privity not required in tort; damages unliquidated in tort; ordinarily no pre-existing relationship needed. Concurrent liability is possible (Donoghue v Stevenson - tort even though contracts existed). TORT vs BREACH OF TRUST: equitable.

Mental element: tort ordinarily needs intention or negligence; some torts are of strict liability (Rylands v Fletcher; absolute liability); motive generally irrelevant (except malicious prosecution, conspiracy, nuisance in some cases). Malice in law = wrongful act done intentionally without just cause; malice in fact = ill will/ spite.

Important maxims: Ubi jus ibi remedium (where there is a right there is a remedy); Volenti non fit injuria; Sic utere tuo ut alienum non laedas (use your own property so as not to harm another); Res ipsa loquitur; Actio personalis moritur cum persona (personal action dies with the person - Sec 306 Indian Succession Act 1925 saves causes of action except defamation, assault and other personal injuries not causing loss to the estate); Respondeat superior; Qui facit per alium facit per se; Damnum sine injuria; Injuria sine damno; Nemo dat; Novus actus interveniens.

Remedies in tort: damages (nominal, contemptuous, general, special, aggravated, exemplary/ punitive), injunction (temporary, perpetual), specific restitution of property, and extra-judicial remedies (self-defence, re-entry, recaption, abatement of nuisance, distress damage feasant).

sections.title: General Defences in Tort
sections.summary: Volenti, necessity, inevitable accident, act of God, private defence, statutory authority and contributory negligence.
key_points: VOLENTI NON FIT INJURIA: a person who voluntarily consents to run a risk of harm cannot complain of it. Requirements: consent must be free and with full knowledge of the nature and extent of the risk (Smith v Baker, 1891: mere knowledge is not consent); the act must be one the consent covers; consent cannot be to an illegal act. Limits: rescue cases - a rescuer is not volenti (Haynes v Harwood, 1935; Wagner v International Railway); sports - participants consent to normal risks (Hall v Brooklands Auto Racing Club, 1933: spectators accept risk of cars leaving the track; Woolridge v Sumner, 1963); passenger with a drunk driver (Dann v Hamilton; later cases - contributory negligence rather than volenti); statutory duty and employer's liability: workman does not consent to employer's breach (Smith v Baker). Consent to surgery: Sec 88, 92 IPC (now BNS Secs 26, 30 - acts done in good faith for benefit).

INEVITABLE ACCIDENT: an event which could not have been avoided by the exercise of ordinary care, caution and skill (Stanley v Powell, 1891: shooting accident). ACT OF GOD: operation of natural forces without human intervention which no reasonable foresight could provide against (Nichols v Marsland, 1876: extraordinary rainfall; Rylands exception). In India courts require the event to be extraordinary: cyclones and floods may or may not qualify depending on foreseeability. PRIVATE DEFENCE: reasonable force to defend person or property (Secs 96-106 IPC; now BNS Secs 34-44); force must be proportionate. NECESSITY: act done to prevent greater harm to the community or to the actor - Cope v Sharpe (1912: burning heather to stop fire); Leigh v Gladstone (forcible feeding of a hunger-striker); public necessity in Sec 81 IPC (BNS Sec 22).

STATUTORY AUTHORITY: an act authorised by statute is not actionable if done without negligence and within the statute (Vaughan v Taff Vale Railway, 1860: sparks from locomotive - no liability as statute authorised the engine and due care was used; Hammersmith Railway v Brand). Absolute statutory authority (when the nuisance is the inevitable result) is a complete defence; conditional authority requires reasonable care. Judicial acts: judges, magistrates have immunity under the Judicial Officers' Protection Act 1850; executive officers' acts; parental and quasi-parental authority (reasonable chastisement); Sec 79 IPC mistake of fact.

PLAINTIFF'S DEFAULT/ CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE: at common law contributory negligence was a complete defence (Butterfield v Forrester, 1809: plaintiff riding fast into an obstruction). The rule was softened by the last opportunity rule (Davies v Mann, 1842: donkey fettered on the highway; defendant had the last opportunity to avoid). In India courts apportion damages (analogous to the English Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945): damages are reduced in proportion to the plaintiff's share of responsibility; apportionment is routine in motor accident claims (the Motor Accident Claims Tribunals reduce compensation by the percentage of contributory negligence; for example 'non-use of helmet or seat belt' - SC cases). Children: lower standard of care; a young child cannot be contributorily negligent. Composite negligence: when two or more wrongdoers cause the same damage, each is liable for the whole; the plaintiff can sue any or all (joint and several liability); contribution among tortfeasors; Khenyei v New India Assurance (2015) clarifies the distinction between contributory and composite negligence in motor claims.

Other defences: LIMITATION (Limitation Act 1963; one year for defamation, false imprisonment and malicious prosecution (Arts 73-76 - verify), three years residuary Art 113); PLAINTIFF'S ILLEGALITY (ex turpi causa non oritur actio); MISTAKE (not generally a defence in tort except in defamation and trespass in limited cases); LEAVE AND LICENCE.

sections.title: Negligence
sections.summary: The most heavily tested tort. Duty of care, standard of care, breach, causation, remoteness, res ipsa loquitur, medical negligence.
key_points: Negligence = breach of a legal duty to take care, resulting in damage to the plaintiff (Alderson B in Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks: omission to do something which a reasonable man would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do). As a TORT, negligence needs: (1) a LEGAL DUTY of care owed by the defendant to the plaintiff; (2) BREACH of that duty; (3) DAMAGE caused by the breach (causation) and not too remote.

DUTY OF CARE: Donoghue v Stevenson (1932, HL): the 'neighbour principle' (Lord Atkin) - you must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour, i.e., persons so closely and directly affected by your act that you ought reasonably to have them in contemplation. A snail in a ginger beer bottle; manufacturer's duty to ultimate consumer. Caparo Industries v Dickman (1990): three-stage test - foreseeability of damage, proximity of relationship, and that it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty. Indian courts follow both; Municipal Corporation of Delhi v Subhagwanti (1966): liability of the corporation for the collapse of a clock tower; res ipsa.

STANDARD OF CARE: the reasonable man (Vaughan v Menlove, 1837 - the objective standard; 'reasonable prudent man'); skilled professionals: standard of the ordinary skilled person exercising that special skill - BOLAM TEST (Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee, 1957): a doctor is not negligent if he acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion. Indian Supreme Court adopts Bolam in Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005) (criminal negligence needs gross negligence/ recklessness - 'rash or negligent act' under Sec 304A IPC, now BNS Sec 106) and Poonam Verma v Ashwin Patel (1996). Informed consent - Samira Kohli v Prabha Manchanda (2008) (consent must be informed; patient must be told of material risks; consent for diagnostic procedure does not cover therapeutic). Children - lower standard; old/ infirm - no lower objective standard.

BREACH: considered with the magnitude of risk, probability of harm, gravity of harm, utility of the act and cost of precautions (Bolton v Stone, 1951: cricket ball hitting a passer-by - risk too remote; Paris v Stepney Borough Council, 1951: greater care to a one-eyed workman; Latimer v AEC, 1953: cost of precautions).

RES IPSA LOQUITUR ('the thing speaks for itself'): where the thing causing the damage is under the management of the defendant, and the accident is such as in the ordinary course of things does not happen if those who have the management use proper care, the accident itself affords reasonable evidence of negligence in the absence of explanation by the defendant. Byrne v Boadle (1863: flour barrel falling from a warehouse window); Scott v London & St Katharine Docks (1865: sugar bags). The maxim shifts the evidentiary burden (not the legal burden) to the defendant. In India it applies in surgery (instrument left inside the body), in aviation, rail and road accidents (Shyam Sunder v State of Rajasthan, 1974: the plaintiff need not prove how the negligence occurred). In medical negligence - V. Kishan Rao v Nikhil Super Speciality Hospital (2010): res ipsa applies in appropriate cases; no need for an expert evidence in every case.

CAUSATION: 'but for' test (Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington Hospital, 1969: arsenic poisoning - hospital's negligence did not cause death as the patient would have died anyway). Novus actus interveniens (new intervening cause) breaks the chain - but a rescuer's or victim's reasonable response doesn't (Scott v Shepherd, 1773 - the squib case). REMOTENESS: Re Polemis (1921) - directness test (all direct consequences even if unforeseeable), now displaced by The Wagon Mound (No 1) (1961, PC): the defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that is reasonably foreseeable (oil spilt on water caught fire due to welding - fire damage not foreseeable). EGGSHELL SKULL RULE: take your victim as you find him (Smith v Leech Brain, 1962; Dulieu v White) - the extent of damage need not be foreseeable if the kind is.

SPECIAL AREAS: (1) Nervous shock/ psychiatric harm (Hambrook v Stokes; Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire - close tie of love and affection, proximity in time and space, direct perception); (2) Negligent misstatement (Hedley Byrne v Heller, 1964 - duty where a special relationship exists and reliance); (3) Pure economic loss; (4) Occupier's liability (invitees, licensees, trespassers; Indian cases apply the common duty of care); (5) Employer's duty - safe system, competent staff, safe premises, adequate plant; (6) Product liability (Donoghue; now CPA 2019 Chapter VI); (7) Professional negligence - doctors, lawyers (Bar of Indian Lawyers v D.K. Gandhi, 2024 - the Court held that advocates' services are outside the CPA 2019 but the decision has been stayed and referred to a larger Bench; verify current status), engineers, architects, banks.

MEDICAL NEGLIGENCE IN INDIA: civil action in tort or under the Consumer Protection Act (Indian Medical Association v V.P. Shantha, 1995 - medical services are 'service' (free services excluded; paid services and contracts of service excluded under personal service)); criminal liability requires gross negligence (Jacob Mathew); doctors are not liable merely because a procedure fails or a more skilful approach existed; liability if (a) lacks the skill professed, or (b) fails to exercise reasonable care. Hospitals vicariously liable for nurses and doctors; Spring Meadows Hospital v Harjol Ahluwalia (1998): the child as patient and parents as consumers; Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v Prasanth S. Dhananka (2009); Martin F. D'Souza v Mohd. Ishfaq (2009): directions that complaints against doctors be examined by a competent doctor's opinion before notice - later refined in V. Kishan Rao (2010) which held that the direction was not mandatory in all cases.
CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE AND COMPOSITE NEGLIGENCE: see 1.2. Negligence in public authorities: State vicarious liability (1.5).

sections.title: Strict and Absolute Liability; Environmental and Hazardous Torts
sections.summary: Rylands v Fletcher, M.C. Mehta (Oleum gas) and the Indian doctrine of absolute liability are near-certain topics.
key_points: RYLANDS v FLETCHER (1868, HL): a person who for his own purposes brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes must keep it at his peril, and, if he does not do so, is prima facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape (Blackburn J). The House of Lords added 'non-natural use' of land. Facts: water from a reservoir flooded the plaintiff's mine through disused shafts.

ESSENTIALS: (1) dangerous thing likely to do mischief if it escapes; (2) ESCAPE from the defendant's land to a place outside his occupation or control (Read v Lyons, 1947: no escape - no liability); (3) NON-NATURAL USE of land (Rickards v Lothian, 1913: ordinary domestic water supply is natural); (4) damage. Mens rea or negligence is unnecessary.

EXCEPTIONS (defences): (1) plaintiff's consent or common benefit; (2) act of God (Nichols v Marsland); (3) act of a stranger (Box v Jubb); (4) statutory authority; (5) default of the plaintiff; (6) in India some courts treat natural use differently, but the main change comes with absolute liability.

ABSOLUTE LIABILITY - M.C. MEHTA v UNION OF INDIA (1987) 1 SCC 395 (Oleum Gas Leak case): after oleum gas leaked from Shriram Foods and Fertiliser Industries in Delhi, the Supreme Court (Bhagwati CJ) held that the Rylands rule, born in the 19th century England, cannot be applied to modern industrial India as is. It laid down the rule of ABSOLUTE LIABILITY: an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity which poses a potential threat to the health and safety of persons working in the factory and residing in the surrounding area owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community to ensure that no harm results to anyone; if harm results, the enterprise is strictly and absolutely liable, WITHOUT the exceptions of Rylands v Fletcher (no defence of act of God or act of a stranger) and without the requirement of 'escape' or 'non-natural use'. The measure of compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise (the 'deep pocket' principle) so that it has a deterrent effect.

Other leading cases: Union Carbide Corporation v Union of India (1989): the Bhopal Gas disaster (1984) was settled for USD 470 million (about Rs 715 crore); the Supreme Court upheld the settlement (1991 review); curative petition seeking additional compensation of about Rs 7,844 crore was dismissed in March 2023. Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act 1985 appointed the Central Government as parens patriae. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v Union of India (1996): 'polluter pays' and absolute liability for hazardous industry; the burden to prove no harm lies on the industry. Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v Union of India (1996): precautionary principle and polluter pays are part of Indian environmental law (Art 21 and Art 48A, 51A(g)). Charan Lal Sahu v Union of India (1990): the state as parens patriae. State of Punjab v Modern Cultivators (1964): Rylands applied to the bursting of a canal.

STATUTORY BACKDROP: Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 - no-fault liability for hazardous substances accidents; owner must take insurance and contribute to the Environmental Relief Fund; National Green Tribunal Act 2010, Sec 17 - NGT can award compensation on the principle of strict liability/ 'no fault' for environmental damage (Sec 17(3) - no fault liability for death/ injury/ damage in accidents involving hazardous substances); Environment (Protection) Act 1986. The NGT Act replaced the National Environment Tribunal Act 1995.

Contrast: Strict liability (Rylands): exceptions available; escape required; non-natural use required. Absolute liability (M.C. Mehta): no exceptions; hazardous industry; no escape requirement; compensation proportional to enterprise capacity. Both are civil liabilities not requiring proof of negligence or intention.

sections.title: Vicarious Liability and Liability of the State; Constitutional Torts
sections.summary: Master-servant, course of employment, sovereign immunity vs State liability and compensation under Arts 32/226.
key_points: VICARIOUS LIABILITY: liability of a person for the torts of another. Basis: respondeat superior; qui facit per alium facit per se. Categories: master and servant (employer liable for torts of an employee committed in the COURSE OF EMPLOYMENT); principal and agent; partners (Partnership Act Sec 18, 25-26); company for acts of its officers; owner for acts of independent contractors in limited cases (non-delegable duties, hazardous operations); parent/ guardian - not automatically.

Tests of employment: control test (master controls the manner of doing the work), integration/ organisation test, multiple factor test; independent contractors - employer generally not liable (exceptions: hazardous works; Rylands; statutory duty; negligent selection; non-delegable duty).

COURSE OF EMPLOYMENT: an act is within the course if it is (a) a wrongful act authorised by the master, or (b) a wrongful and unauthorised mode of doing some act authorised by the master (Limpus v London General Omnibus Co, 1862: bus driver racing against another bus in violation of instructions; Century Insurance v Northern Ireland Road Transport Board, 1942: driver smoking while unloading petrol). The master is NOT liable if the act is wholly outside employment (a 'frolic of his own' - Joel v Morison). Lord Phillips: 'close connection' test in Lister v Hesley Hall (2001) for intentional wrongs. Indian courts apply the same principles to motor accidents: an owner is vicariously liable for a driver's negligence in the course of employment.

LIABILITY OF THE STATE: Art 300(1): the Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India, subject to any law enacted; the liability is the same as that of the Dominion/ Province before the Constitution. Historical: P. & O. Steam Navigation Co v Secretary of State for India (1861, Calcutta SC): State not liable for tortious acts done in exercise of sovereign powers but liable for acts of commercial/ non-sovereign nature (maintenance of a dockyard). Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v State of UP (1965): police officers seized gold and a constable misappropriated it; the State was held NOT liable as the power to seize was a sovereign power; the Court urged legislation. State of Rajasthan v Vidyawati (1962): State liable for the negligence of a driver of a Government jeep. The distinction between sovereign and non-sovereign functions has been progressively diluted: State of Gujarat v Memon Mahomed Haji Hasam (1967); Smt. Basava Kom Dyamogouda Patil v State of Mysore (1977); N. Nagendra Rao & Co v State of Andhra Pradesh (1994): State liable for loss caused by negligence of officials in storing goods seized - the sovereign immunity doctrine is outdated and applies only to inalienable sovereign functions such as defence, war, and legislative functions; Saheli v Commissioner of Police, Delhi (1990): State liable to pay compensation for death caused by police; custodial death. Immunity under the Constitution: the President and Governors (Art 361) personally.

CONSTITUTIONAL TORT / PUBLIC LAW COMPENSATION: the Supreme Court and High Courts award monetary compensation under Arts 32 and 226 for violation of fundamental rights, particularly Art 21, as public law remedy (distinct from private tort damages): Rudul Sah v State of Bihar (1983): compensation for illegal detention for 14 years after acquittal; Bhim Singh v State of J&K (1985): MLA unlawfully detained; Sebastian M. Hongray v Union of India (1984): exemplary costs for disappearance of persons; Nilabati Behera v State of Orissa (1993): custodial death - compensation as public law remedy, sovereign immunity not a defence; D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal (1997): guidelines on arrest and detention; custodial violence; the State is liable to pay compensation. The remedy is without prejudice to civil/ criminal action. Also: compensation for wrongful acts by police in encounters (PUCL v State of Maharashtra, 2014 guidelines); and for medical negligence in government hospitals (Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v State of West Bengal, 1996 - right to emergency medical treatment, Art 21).

Government contracts and torts: Sec 80 CPC: notice of 2 months before suing the Government (exception: urgent relief with leave, Sec 80(2)); Limitation: as in the general law. Public authorities' liability for statutory duties: ordinary law of tort (negligence, nuisance, breach of statutory duty). Tort of misfeasance in public office.

sections.title: Nuisance and Trespass
sections.summary: Public and private nuisance; essentials, defences, remedies; trespass to person, land and goods.
key_points: NUISANCE: an unlawful interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land, or of some right over or in connection with it. PRIVATE NUISANCE: unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of land (actionable on proof of damage - sensible personal discomfort or physical damage to property; no need for trespass). PUBLIC NUISANCE: an act or omission which materially affects the reasonable comfort and convenience of a class of Her Majesty's subjects; also a crime (Sec 268 IPC, now BNS Sec 270); a private individual can sue only if he suffers 'special damage' over and above the general public (Sec 91 CPC - suit with the Advocate General's leave/ two persons with court's leave).

ESSENTIALS OF PRIVATE NUISANCE: (1) an unreasonable and substantial interference; (2) the interference must be with the use and enjoyment of land; (3) actual damage. Types: physical damage to property (St Helen's Smelting Co v Tipping, 1865 - fumes damaging trees; a higher standard for property damage than for personal discomfort, which is judged by the character of the locality) and interference with comfort (smell, noise, vibration). 'Sticky' factors: locality (Sturges v Bridgman, 1879: 'what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey'); duration; sensitivity of the plaintiff (Robinson v Kilvert: abnormally sensitive trade not protected); malice (Christie v Davey, 1893: banging walls in response to music lessons; Hollywood Silver Fox Farm v Emmett, 1936: gun shots to disturb foxes); utility is no defence.

DEFENCES: prescription (20 years' continuous enjoyment of the nuisance as of right - Sec 15 Easements Act); statutory authority; consent; coming to the nuisance is NOT a defence (Sturges v Bridgman); act of a stranger; inevitable accident; public benefit/ utility is not a defence. REMEDIES: damages; injunction; abatement (self-help, with notice, without causing unnecessary damage). Indian cases: Ushaben v Bhagyalakshmi Chitra Mandir (1978, Gujarat HC): screening of the film 'Jai Santoshi Maa' hurt religious feelings but was not a nuisance as no interference with enjoyment of land; Radhey Shyam v Gur Prasad (1978 All HC): flour mill's noise/ vibration; Municipal Council, Ratlam v Vardichan (1980): SC compelled the municipality to remove open drains under Sec 133 CrPC (now BNSS Sec 152) - public nuisance and the duty of local bodies cannot be defeated by financial inability; Sec 133 CrPC conditional order of Magistrate for removal of public nuisance (BNSS Sec 152).

TRESPASS: direct interference with the person, goods or land of the plaintiff, actionable per se (without proof of damage). Trespass to the person: assault (apprehension of immediate harmful contact; words alone do not constitute assault if accompanied by no act), battery (direct application of force; hostility not essential - Collins v Wilcock), false imprisonment (total restraint of liberty without lawful justification - Bird v Jones, 1845: partial obstruction is not imprisonment; Meering v Grahame-White Aviation, 1920: restraint without knowledge). Remedy: habeas corpus and damages (Rudul Sah; Bhim Singh). Trespass to land: unauthorised entry/ remaining/ placing anything on the land; the plaintiff needs possession (not ownership); trespass ab initio (Six Carpenters' Case, 1610); remedies: damages, injunction, ejectment, mesne profits (Sec 2(12) CPC), Sec 6 Specific Relief Act (summary possession), self-help re-entry (limited). Defences: licence, necessity, justification by law, private defence. Entick v Carrington (1765): a state officer's entry without legal authority is trespass. Trespass to goods: direct interference with chattels in possession; conversion (dealing with goods inconsistent with the owner's right); detinue (wrongful detention).

sections.title: Defamation, Malicious Prosecution, Deceit and Other Torts
sections.summary: Libel vs slander, defences (truth, fair comment, privilege), malicious prosecution essentials, conspiracy, passing off, privacy.
key_points: DEFAMATION: publication of a false statement which tends to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society, or cause him to be shunned or avoided, or exposes him to hatred, contempt or ridicule. ESSENTIALS: (1) the statement must be defamatory; (2) it must refer to the plaintiff; (3) it must be PUBLISHED to a third person (publication to the plaintiff alone is not publication - Mahendra Ram v Harnandan Prasad, 1958: letter in Urdu). LIBEL: defamation in permanent form (writing, print, pictures, effigies) - actionable per se and also a crime. SLANDER: defamation in transient form (spoken words, gestures) - actionable only on proof of special damage, except four classes: imputation of a crime punishable with imprisonment, loathsome disease, unchastity of a woman (in England by statute), and imputation affecting the plaintiff's office, profession, trade or business. In India, the distinction between libel and slander is not maintained for the criminal law (Sec 499 IPC - now BNS Sec 356 - covers both); in civil law the English distinction is applied by many courts, though several High Courts have treated slander as actionable per se (Indian courts have not definitely settled the issue).

CRIMINAL DEFAMATION: Sec 499/500 IPC (now BNS Sec 356); upheld as constitutional in Subramanian Swamy v Union of India (2016) (reasonable restriction on Art 19(1)(a) to protect reputation under Art 21). Sec 499 exceptions: truth for the public good, public servant's conduct, conduct of any person touching public question, publication of reports of courts, merits of a case decided, merits of public performance, censure by person having authority, accusation in good faith to authorised person, imputation made in good faith for protection of one's own interests, caution conveyed in good faith.

DEFENCES IN DEFAMATION: (1) JUSTIFICATION/ TRUTH (civil: truth is a complete defence; criminal: truth must also be for the public good); (2) FAIR COMMENT on a matter of public interest - based on facts truly stated, honest opinion without malice; (3) PRIVILEGE: absolute privilege (statements in Parliament/ legislature, judicial proceedings (judges, witnesses, counsel), official communications, communications between spouses (Evidence Act Sec 122)) and qualified privilege (statements made in discharge of a duty or protecting an interest, reports of proceedings (newspapers), statements to police; defeated by malice); (4) CONSENT; (5) APOLOGY (mitigation). R. Rajagopal v State of Tamil Nadu (1994): public officials' actions; no prior restraint; publication of matters of public record is permitted; privacy and Art 21.

MALICIOUS PROSECUTION: ESSENTIALS (Mohamed Amin v Jogendra Kumar Bannerjee, 1947 PC): (1) the defendant prosecuted the plaintiff (set the law in motion) - criminal proceedings; (2) the prosecution ended in the plaintiff's FAVOUR (termination); (3) it was without REASONABLE AND PROBABLE CAUSE; (4) it was actuated by MALICE (an improper motive); (5) damage to reputation, person/ liberty, or property (costs). Contrast: abuse of process (misuse of legal process for a collateral object); malicious civil proceedings (needs special damage); FALSE IMPRISONMENT vs MALICIOUS PROSECUTION: in false imprisonment the detention is without lawful authority; in malicious prosecution the process is regular but maliciously invoked.

OTHER TORTS: DECEIT (fraudulent misrepresentation causing damage - Derry v Peek, 1889); CONSPIRACY (agreement to injure; Quinn v Leathem); INDUCING BREACH OF CONTRACT (Lumley v Gye, 1853); INTIMIDATION; INJURIOUS FALSEHOOD/ trade libel; PASSING OFF (misrepresentation causing damage to goodwill - see Part 8 IP module); BREACH OF STATUTORY DUTY; INTERFERENCE with privacy - K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017): right to privacy is a fundamental right under Art 21; common law invasion of privacy tort developing (R. Rajagopal); NEGLIGENT MISSTATEMENT; OCCUPIERS' LIABILITY; nervous shock; wrongful birth. Interference with employment: the 'tort of interference with contractual relations' - Lumley v Gye; Indian recognition by High Courts (e.g., in competition/ trade contexts).

INTERNET AND AI-ERA TORTS (hot): personality rights and deepfakes - the Delhi and Bombay High Courts have repeatedly granted injunctions to celebrities against AI-generated deepfakes and misuse of voice/ likeness (2026 orders protecting e.g. Swami Ramdev and Sonakshi Sinha); defamation on social media - intermediaries' safe-harbour under Sec 79 IT Act subject to the IT Rules; the tort of passing off for personality (Titan Industries v Ramkumar Jewellers, 2012; Anil Kapoor v Simply Life, 2023). These topics are expected to feature in any 'recent developments' question.

sections.title: Remedies, Damages, Joint Tortfeasors and Fatal Accidents
sections.summary: Heads of damages, exemplary damages, Fatal Accidents Act and apportionment.
key_points: KINDS OF DAMAGES: nominal (right violated, no loss), contemptuous (technical win, worthless claim), general (presumed loss: pain and suffering), special (proved pecuniary loss), aggravated (injury to feelings due to malice/ insult), EXEMPLARY/ PUNITIVE (to punish and deter): Rookes v Devlin (1964) restricted exemplary damages to (i) oppressive, arbitrary or unconstitutional action by government servants, (ii) conduct calculated to make profit exceeding compensation, and (iii) cases authorised by statute. Indian courts award exemplary damages for constitutional torts (Rudul Sah; Nilabati) and in environmental disasters (M.C. Mehta).

PERSONAL INJURY HEADS: pecuniary - medical expenses, loss of earnings, loss of earning capacity, cost of future care; non-pecuniary - pain and suffering, loss of amenities, loss of expectation of life. Death: Fatal Accidents Act 1855 - the dependants (wife, husband, parent, child) can sue for the pecuniary loss from the death caused by wrongful act, neglect or default of another; the action is for the benefit of the dependants and is brought by the personal representative or by dependants (Sec 1A - the dependants can sue where no representative sues within six months). Under the Motor Vehicles Act the Claims Tribunals follow tort principles (see MV module). Doctrine: actio personalis moritur cum persona saved by Sec 306 Succession Act. Survival of action vs dependency claim: the estate's claim (loss to the estate) vs dependants' claim (loss of dependency).

JOINT TORTFEASORS: persons who commit the same tort together (concerted action, common design, or vicarious relation) - each is liable for the whole damage; the plaintiff may sue all or any; release of one does not release others; contribution among tortfeasors (English Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978; in India principles of equity). INDEPENDENT/ SEVERAL TORTFEASORS causing the same damage: each liable for the whole damage; apportionment by the court.

REMEDIES BY ACT OF PARTIES: self-defence; recaption; re-entry; abatement of nuisance; distress damage feasant (seizing trespassing animals); expulsion of trespasser. JUDICIAL REMEDIES: damages; injunction (Specific Relief Act Secs 36-42; Order XXXIX CPC); restitution (Specific Relief Act Secs 5-8).

LIMITATION: Limitation Act 1963 - one year (libel, slander, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution); three years residuary (Art 113 - negligence, nuisance, trespass where no specific article, injunction); continuing wrongs (Sec 22); Sec 17 fraud; Sec 5 condonation. Death/ injury claims under MV Act: no limitation after 1 April 2022 for claim applications (Sec 166(3) was omitted by the 2019 Amendment, brought into force 1 April 2022). Consumer claims: two years (Sec 69 CPA 2019).

sections.title: Overview, Definitions, Licensing and Registration
sections.summary: The Motor Vehicles Act 1988 as amended by the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019 (effective in phases from 1 September 2019). Know the definitions, age limits and the major registration/licensing rules.
key_points: The MV Act 1988 replaced the 1939 Act. It regulates licensing of drivers and conductors, registration, permits, control of traffic, insurance against third-party risks, liability without fault, Motor Accident Claims Tribunals, offences and penalties. The 2019 Amendment was a major overhaul: higher penalties, Good Samaritan protection (Sec 134A), Motor Vehicle Accident Fund (Sec 164B), cashless treatment in the golden hour (Sec 162), interim relief scheme (Sec 164A), hit-and-run compensation, removal of the 6-month limit on claims (Sec 166(3) omitted), liability of juveniles' guardians (Sec 199A), recall of defective vehicles (Sec 110A), aggregators (Sec 93), National Transportation Policy and electronic monitoring.

KEY DEFINITIONS (Sec 2): 'motor vehicle' = any mechanically propelled vehicle adapted for use upon roads whether power is transmitted from an external or internal source (Sec 2(28)); excludes vehicles running on fixed rails or used solely in a factory/ enclosed premises, and vehicles with less than 4 wheels and engine capacity not exceeding 25 cc (Sec 2(28) as amended); 'public place' (Sec 2(34)) = a road, street, way or other place, whether a thoroughfare or not, to which the public have a right of access, and includes any place or stand at which passengers are picked up; 'owner' (Sec 2(30)) = the person in whose name the vehicle is registered and includes, where the person is a minor, the guardian; in relation to hire purchase/ agreement of lease/ hypothecation, the person in possession of the vehicle under that agreement; 'light motor vehicle' (Sec 2(21)) = transport vehicle or omnibus the gross vehicle weight of either of which or a motor car or tractor or road roller the unladen weight of any of which does not exceed 7,500 kg; 'transport vehicle' (Sec 2(47)) = public service vehicle, goods carriage, educational institution bus or private service vehicle; 'driver', 'driving licence', 'learner's licence', 'goods carriage', 'stage carriage', 'contract carriage', 'taxi cab', 'aggregator' (a digital intermediary or market place for a passenger to connect with a driver for transportation), 'trailer', 'permit'.

LICENSING (Chapter II, Secs 3-28): Sec 3: no person shall drive a motor vehicle in any public place unless he holds an effective driving licence authorising him to drive the vehicle; transport vehicle - licence must specifically authorise (Sec 3(1)). Sec 4: AGE LIMIT - a person under 18 cannot drive a motor vehicle in a public place; exception: a person above 16 can drive a motor cycle with engine capacity not exceeding 50 cc; a person under 20 cannot drive a transport vehicle (verify the exceptions for transport vehicles in the bare Act). Sec 7: learner's licence; Sec 8: grant of learner's licence; Sec 9: grant of driving licence - applicant must pass a test of competence; Sec 14: currency - non-transport vehicle: 20 years or until the holder attains 40 years, whichever is earlier; Sec 15: renewal; Sec 19: power of licensing authority to disqualify; Sec 20: power of court to disqualify; Sec 21: suspension; Sec 22: suspension/ cancellation on being found not fit. Licence can be digital (DigiLocker). Sec 14(2)(b) transport vehicle: 3 years.

REGISTRATION (Chapter IV, Secs 39-65): Sec 39: no person shall drive a motor vehicle (and no owner shall cause or permit it to be driven) in any public place or any other place unless the vehicle is registered in accordance with the Chapter and the certificate of registration has not been suspended or cancelled (except temporary registration, Sec 43); Sec 41: registration process; certificate of registration; Sec 47: assignment of new registration mark when a vehicle is removed to another State - within 12 months; Sec 50: transfer of ownership - the transferor must report within 14 days; transferee within 30 days; Sec 51: hypothecation; Sec 52: alteration of vehicle needs the registering authority's approval; Sec 56: certificate of fitness for transport vehicles. PERMITS (Chapter V): Sec 66: necessity for permits for transport vehicles; Sec 67: State control; Sec 72-74: stage carriage, contract carriage; goods carriage permits (Sec 79-82); national permit (Sec 88(9)); Sec 93: licensing of aggregators (2019).

CONTROL OF TRAFFIC (Chapter VII-VIII): Sec 112: speed limits fixed by the Central/ State Government; Sec 113: limits of weight and limitations on use; Sec 115: power to restrict conveyance of goods; Sec 119: duty to obey traffic signs; Sec 128: safety measures for drivers and pillion riders of two-wheelers - no more than one pillion rider; Sec 129: wearing of protective headgear (helmet) for drivers and pillion riders of two-wheelers (exempt: Sikhs wearing turban); Sec 138(3): safety belts for car occupants; Sec 134: DUTY OF DRIVER IN CASE OF ACCIDENT - where bodily injury to a person or damage to property of a third party, or damage to any animal, is caused due to an accident in which a motor vehicle is involved, the driver or other person in charge of the vehicle shall (a) unless it is not practicable to do so on account of mob fury or any other reason beyond his control, take all reasonable steps to secure medical attention for the injured person, by conveying him to the nearest medical practitioner or hospital, and it shall be the duty of every registered medical practitioner or the doctor on duty in the hospital immediately to attend to the injured person and render medical aid or treatment without waiting for any procedural formalities, unless the injured person or his guardian, in case he is a minor, desires otherwise; (b) give on demand by a police officer any information required by him, or, if no police officer is present, report the circumstances of the occurrence, including the circumstances, if any, which prevented him from complying with the requirement of clause (a), at the nearest police station as soon as possible, and in any case within 24 hours of the occurrence; (c) give the following information in writing to the insurer, who has issued the certificate of insurance, about the occurrence of the accident, namely: insurance policy number and period of its validity; date, time and place of accident; particulars of persons injured or killed; name of the driver and the particulars of his driving licence.

GOOD SAMARITANS - Sec 134A (inserted 2019): a Good Samaritan shall not be liable for any civil or criminal action for any injury to or death of the victim of an accident involving a motor vehicle where such injury or death resulted from the Good Samaritan's negligence in acting or failing to act while rendering emergency medical or non-medical care or assistance. 'Good Samaritan' = a person who in good faith, voluntarily and without expectation of payment or reward renders emergency medical or non-medical care or assistance at the scene of an accident to the victim or conveys such victim to the hospital. The Sec 134A is backed by the Supreme Court's Save Life Foundation v Union of India (2016), whose guidelines (no compulsion to disclose identity, no detention at hospital, no demand for payment) were codified. In May 2026 the Supreme Court (SaveLife Foundation v Union of India, order dated 26 May 2026) issued detailed directions on emergency response, golden hour care and operationalisation of the cashless scheme within three months.

Registration is compulsory (Sec 39); transfer reporting - 14 days.

sections.title: Insurance against Third-Party Risks (Chapter XI, Secs 145-164)
sections.summary: Compulsory insurance and the insurer's liability are heavily tested: Sec 146, 147, 149, 'pay and recover', defences available to insurer.
key_points: Sec 146 NECESSITY FOR INSURANCE: no person shall use, except as a passenger, or cause or allow any other person to use, a motor vehicle in a public place unless there is in force in relation to the use of the vehicle by that person or that other person, as the case may be, a policy of insurance complying with the requirements of this Chapter. Exception: vehicles owned by the Central/ State Government and used for Government purposes unconnected with commercial enterprise. The insurance requirement is compulsory third-party (Act-only) cover.

Sec 147 REQUIREMENTS OF POLICIES: the policy must be issued by an authorised insurer and must insure the person (owner) or classes of persons specified, against any liability which may be incurred in respect of the death of or bodily injury to any person (including owner of the goods or his authorised representative carried in the vehicle) or damage to any property of a third party caused by or arising out of the use of the vehicle in a public place; and against the death of or bodily injury to any passenger of a public service vehicle caused by or arising out of the use of the vehicle. The policy is not required to cover liability in respect of death or injury arising out of and in the course of employment of the employee (workmen's compensation liability is otherwise covered), the death or bodily injury to the owner's employee other than the driver/ conductor/ ticket examiner; and contractual liability. Limit: unlimited for death or bodily injury; for third-party property damage, the limit is fixed (as per the Central Government rules; under the IRDAI regime the policy covers property damage up to Rs 7.5 lakh as per tariff - verify). Gratuitous passengers: the Supreme Court's decisions (New India Assurance v Asha Rani, 2003 and later cases) address whether the statutory policy covers gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles; verify the current position before answering.

Sec 149 DUTY OF INSURERS TO SATISFY JUDGMENTS AND AWARDS AGAINST PERSONS INSURED IN RESPECT OF THIRD PARTY RISKS: if, after a certificate of insurance has been issued, a judgment or award is obtained in respect of any liability required to be covered by a policy under Sec 147, the insurer shall, notwithstanding that the insurer may be entitled to avoid or cancel the policy, pay to the person entitled to the benefit of the decree any sum not exceeding the sum assured payable thereunder, as if he were the judgment debtor, in respect of the liability, together with any amount payable in respect of costs and any sum payable in respect of interest. Sec 149(2): no sum is payable by an insurer in respect of any judgment unless before the commencement of the proceedings in which the judgment is given the insurer had notice through the Court or the claimant; and the insurer may defend only on the SPECIFIED GROUNDS: (a) that there has been a breach of a specified condition of the policy, being one of the following: (i) a condition excluding the use of the vehicle (A) for hire or reward where the vehicle is on the date of the contract of insurance a vehicle not covered by a permit to ply for hire or reward; (B) for organised racing and speed testing; (C) for a purpose not allowed by the permit under which the vehicle is used where the vehicle is a transport vehicle; (D) without side-car being attached where the vehicle is a motor cycle; or (ii) a condition excluding driving by a named person or persons or by any person who is not duly licensed, or by any person who has been disqualified for holding or obtaining a driving licence during the period of disqualification; or (iii) a condition excluding liability for injury caused or contributed to by conditions of war, civil war, riot or civil commotion; or (b) that the policy is void on the ground that it was obtained by the non-disclosure of a material fact or by a representation of fact which was false in some material particular. The insurer's right is subject to proof that the breach was FUNDAMENTAL and was the cause of the accident, and burden lies on the insurer.

'PAY AND RECOVER' DOCTRINE: National Insurance Co Ltd v Swaran Singh (2004) (three-Judge Bench): where the driver has a fake or invalid licence, the insurer is liable to pay the third-party claimant but may recover the amount from the owner IF the owner is shown to have been at fault - i.e., the insurer must prove that the owner was aware of the invalidity or failed to verify the licence; mere absence of valid licence is not by itself a ground to deny the third party claim; the Tribunal can direct the insurer to pay first and recover from the insured/ owner (this is the 'pay and recover' principle). In Mukund Dewangan v Oriental Insurance (2017) (three-judge Bench), the Court held that a driver holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle (LMV) is entitled to drive a transport vehicle of that class whose gross vehicle weight does not exceed 7,500 kg without a separate endorsement; the insurer cannot deny liability on that ground. A November 2024 five-judge Bench decision (Bajaj Allianz General Insurance v Rambha Devi, November 2024) reaffirmed Mukund Dewangan: LMV licence holders can drive light transport vehicles up to 7,500 kg GVW. The principle: an insurer cannot avoid liability to a third party; it may only avoid the insured's indemnity if specific breach is proved.

OTHER INSURANCE POINTS: Sec 148: settlement between insurers and insured persons; Sec 150: rights of third parties against insurers on insolvency of the insured; Sec 151: duty to give information as to insurance; Sec 152: settlement between insurer and insured persons; Sec 156: effect of death on certain causes of action; Sec 157: transfer of certificate of insurance - the certificate of insurance and the policy described therein are deemed to have been transferred in favour of the person to whom the motor vehicle is transferred (deemed transfer, with the transferee to apply within 14 days for the necessary changes). Insurers can also be impleaded (Sec 170). A 'no fault' claim and a 'fault' claim can be pursued (see 2.3).

sections.title: Liability without Fault, Hit-and-Run, Structured Formula and Interim Relief (Secs 140-144, 161-164B)
sections.summary: No-fault liability (Sec 140), structured formula (Sec 163A), hit-and-run (Sec 161), and the newest schemes (Secs 162, 164A, 164B).
key_points: Sec 140 LIABILITY TO PAY COMPENSATION IN CERTAIN CASES ON THE PRINCIPLE OF NO FAULT: where death or permanent disablement of any person has resulted from an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle or motor vehicles, the owner of the vehicle shall, jointly and severally, be liable to pay compensation in respect of such death or disablement in accordance with the provisions of this section. The amount: Rs 50,000 in respect of the death of any person, and Rs 25,000 in respect of the permanent disablement of any person (as increased by the 2019 Amendment; earlier Rs 25,000/ Rs 12,000). The claimant does not need to plead or establish that the death or permanent disablement was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of the owner or of any other person (Sec 140(3)). The compensation under Sec 140 is in addition to any other compensation (the amount paid is deducted from the final award - Sec 141). Sec 142: permanent disablement: loss of sight, loss of limbs/ permanent loss of use; Sec 143: applicability to transport vehicles; Sec 144: overriding effect.

Sec 163A SPECIAL PROVISIONS AS TO PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION ON STRUCTURED FORMULA BASIS: notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or any other law, the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer shall be liable to pay in the case of death or permanent disablement due to accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, compensation, as indicated in the Second Schedule, to the legal heirs or the victim, as the case may be. It is a no-fault claim: the claimant is not required to plead or establish that the death or disablement was due to any wrongful act or negligence of the owner or driver. Deepal Girishbhai Soni v United India Insurance (2004): Sec 163A is a special provision that overrides Sec 166; a claimant who elects Sec 163A cannot claim Sec 166 (and vice versa: the claimant must elect); the structured formula is a final compensation; in Sec 163A claims, negligence/ contributory negligence is irrelevant. The structured formula is in the Second Schedule (originally for victims with annual income up to Rs 40,000 - verify the current position). In Sec 163A proceedings the defence of contributory negligence is not available.

Sec 161 SPECIAL PROVISIONS AS TO COMPENSATION IN CASE OF HIT AND RUN MOTOR ACCIDENTS: 'hit and run motor accident' means an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle or motor vehicles the identity whereof cannot be ascertained in spite of reasonable efforts for the purpose. The Central Government/ Solatium Fund (now Motor Vehicle Accident Fund under Sec 164B) pays: Rs 2,00,000 (2 lakh) in the case of death and Rs 50,000 in the case of grievous hurt (the amounts under the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019, brought into force on 1 April 2022 by the Central Motor Vehicles (Compensation of Victims of Hit and Run Motor Accidents) Scheme 2022). Previously Rs 25,000 and Rs 12,500 (Solatium Scheme 1989). Compensation under Sec 161 is not payable if the claim is covered by other schemes.

Sec 162: INSURERS' DUTY TO PROVIDE CASHLESS TREATMENT during the GOLDEN HOUR (the time period lasting one hour from the time of traumatic injury, during which prompt medical treatment has the highest likelihood of preventing death - the definition in the Explanation); the Central Government shall make a scheme for the cashless treatment of victims of road accidents during the golden hour. After the Supreme Court's repeated directions (S. Rajaseekaran v Union of India; January 2025 order of Justices Abhay S. Oka and Ujjal Bhuyan), the Central Government notified the Cashless Treatment of Road Accident Victims Scheme, 2025 on 5 May 2025 (treatment up to Rs 1.5 lakh per victim for a maximum of seven days from the date of the accident). By a notification of 19 February 2026 (S.O. 951(E)) the scheme has been renamed the 'Prime Minister - Road Accident Victims' Hospitalisation and Assured Treatment (PM-RAHAT) Scheme'. In SaveLife Foundation v Union of India (26 May 2026) the Supreme Court directed the full operationalisation of PM-RAHAT within three months along with other emergency care directions.

Sec 164A: SCHEME FOR INTERIM RELIEF to victims: the Central Government may make a scheme for interim relief to the victims of road accidents (pending final compensation). Sec 164A came into force on 1 April 2022 but the scheme was not framed for a long time (the Supreme Court criticised the delay). The Central Government has now framed the Compensation to Victims (Interim Relief) Scheme, 2026; in August 2026 the Supreme Court expressed surprise at its 'quiet' rollout (called it an 'unannounced law') and directed wide publicity; the amicus curiae pointed out that the scheme applies only to insured vehicles where the insurance company pays. Sec 164B: MOTOR VEHICLE ACCIDENT FUND - constituted by the Central Government (replacing the Solatium Fund of Sec 161(3) scheme); utilised for (a) treatment of persons injured in road accidents in accordance with the Sec 162 scheme, (b) compensation to representatives of deceased persons in hit-and-run cases, (c) compensation to grievously hurt persons in hit-and-run cases, (d) compensation to victims of accidents where the Sec 140 conditions apply/ for interim relief, (e) other purposes as prescribed. Central Motor Vehicles (Motor Vehicle Accident Fund) Rules 2022; the Fund is financed by a cess/ contributions (including from insurers and a percentage of premium) and Government grants.

sections.title: Motor Accident Claims Tribunals and Computation of Compensation (Secs 165-176)
sections.summary: Procedure (Secs 165-176) and the Supreme Court's compensation framework (Sarla Verma, Pranay Sethi) are the top-yield areas.
key_points: Sec 165: constitution of Claims Tribunals by the State Government for the area, adjudicating upon claims for compensation arising out of accidents involving the death of, or bodily injury to, persons arising out of the use of motor vehicles, or damages to any property of a third party so arising, or both. Tribunal: members - a sitting/ retired High Court judge, a District Judge or an Additional District Judge. Sec 175: BAR OF JURISDICTION OF CIVIL COURTS - where any Claims Tribunal has been constituted for any area, no Civil Court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any question relating to any claim for compensation which may be adjudicated upon by the Claims Tribunal for that area.

Sec 166 APPLICATION FOR COMPENSATION: made (a) by the person who has sustained the injury; or (b) by the owner of the property; or (c) where death has resulted from the accident, by all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased; or (d) by any agent duly authorised by the person injured or all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased. Where all the legal representatives have not joined, the application shall be made on behalf of or for the benefit of all and the legal representatives who have not joined shall be impleaded as respondents. Sec 166(2): the application is made to the Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the area in which the accident occurred, or to the Claims Tribunal within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the claimant resides or carries on business or within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the defendant resides (as amended in 2019). Sec 166(3) (the six-month limit) was omitted by the 2019 Amendment, with effect from 1 April 2022. Sec 166(4): the Claims Tribunal shall treat any report of accidents forwarded to it under Sec 158(6) as an application for compensation under this Act (2019 amendment). Sec 158(6): the police officer must forward the Detailed Accident Report (DAR) within 30 days to the Claims Tribunal and the insurer; Sec 159: duty of police officers to prepare a DAR within 48 hours (Form of report by the police: Central Motor Vehicles Rules). The Supreme Court in Gohar Mohammed v UPSRTC (2022) gave directions on DAR/ Form-based claims.

Sec 167: OPTION regarding claims for compensation in certain cases - where the death of or bodily injury to any person gives rise to a claim for compensation under this Act and also under the Workmen's Compensation Act 1923, the person entitled to compensation may, without prejudice to the provisions of Chapter X (no-fault liability), claim such compensation under either of those Acts but not under both. Sec 168: AWARD OF THE CLAIMS TRIBUNAL - on receipt of an application for compensation made under Sec 166, the Claims Tribunal shall, after giving notice of the application to the insurer and after giving the parties (including the insurer) an opportunity of being heard, hold an inquiry into the claim or, as the case may be, each of the claims and, subject to the provisions of Sec 162 may make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be JUST and specifying the person or persons to whom compensation shall be paid; the Tribunal shall specify the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be. Sec 169: PROCEDURE AND POWERS - the Tribunal may follow such summary procedure as it thinks fit; it has the powers of a Civil Court for summoning witnesses, enforcing attendance, discovery and production of documents (the Tribunal is not bound by the strict rules of procedure and evidence - proof on preponderance of probability; the standard of proof in claims is preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt - Bimla Devi v Himachal Road Transport Corporation, 2009). Sec 170: IMPLEADING INSURERS in claims for compensation - where in the course of any inquiry the insurer is given notice of the application, he may, with the previous permission in writing of the Tribunal, contest the claim on any of the grounds in Sec 149(2) (or on the grounds that there's collusion between the person making the claim and the person against whom the claim is made, or the person against whom the claim is made has failed to contest the claim). Sec 171: AWARD OF INTEREST where any claim is allowed - the Tribunal may direct that in addition to the amount of compensation simple interest shall also be paid at such rate and from such date not earlier than the date of making the claim as it may specify (courts commonly award 7.5% to 9% p.a.). Sec 172: AWARD OF COMPENSATORY COSTS in certain cases (false or vexatious claims or defences). Sec 173: APPEAL - any person aggrieved by an award of a Claims Tribunal may, within ninety days from the date of the award, prefer an appeal to the High Court (the High Court may entertain after 90 days if sufficient cause); no appeal by a person who is required to pay any amount in terms of such award shall be entertained by the High Court unless he has deposited with it twenty-five thousand rupees or fifty per cent of the amount so awarded, whichever is less, in the manner directed by the High Court. Sec 174: RECOVERY of money from insurer as arrears of land revenue (the Claims Tribunal issues a certificate to the Collector). Sec 176: power of the State Government to make rules.

COMPUTATION OF COMPENSATION - MULTIPLIER METHOD (Sec 168 'just compensation'): General Manager, Kerala SRTC v Susamma Thomas (1994) adopted the multiplier method; Sarla Verma v Delhi Transport Corporation (2009): standardised the multiplier (age-wise table: 18 for 15-20 years, 17 for 21-25, 18 for 26-30, 17 for 31-35, 16 for 36-40, 15 for 41-45, 13 for 46-50, 11 for 51-55, 9 for 56-60, 7 for 61-65, 5 for 66-70), and the deduction for personal expenses of the deceased: 1/3 where the dependants are 2-3, 1/4 where 4-6, 1/5 where more than 6; for a bachelor, 50% deducted (parents dependent: personal expense 50%); in the case of a married deceased with a dependent spouse, 1/3. National Insurance Co v Pranay Sethi (2017) (five-Judge Bench): FUTURE PROSPECTS must be added to the established income of the deceased - for those with a permanent job: 50% if the deceased was below 40 years, 30% if 40-50 years, 15% if 50-60 years; for self-employed or fixed-wage persons: 40% (below 40), 25% (40-50), 10% (50-60) (no addition above 60). Conventional heads: loss of estate - Rs 15,000; funeral expenses - Rs 15,000; loss of consortium (spousal) - Rs 40,000, with a 10% enhancement every three years. Magma General Insurance v Nanu Ram (2018): loss of consortium extends to parental and filial consortium (children and parents): Rs 40,000 each. Raj Kumar v Ajay Kumar (2011): injury cases - functional disability and loss of earning capacity: the Tribunal must assess the percentage of permanent disability as regards the specific injured person's profession; heads include pain and suffering, medical expenses, attendant charges, loss of amenities, future medical expenses. Notional income for non-earning housewife/ children: courts adopt a notional income (e.g., Lata Wadhwa v State of Bihar - Rs 3,000 per month; Arun Kumar Agrawal v National Insurance (2010) value of services of a homemaker; Kirti v Oriental Insurance (2020)). Interest: simple, 9% in many cases (Supreme Court guidance varies).

NEGLIGENCE/ BURDEN: the claimant must prove negligence of the driver (not required in Sec 140/ 163A claims) by preponderance of probabilities; res ipsa loquitur is applicable in some cases (e.g., a bus falling from a bridge); police charge-sheet is not conclusive (a FIR/ charge sheet can be used as evidence of negligence); acquittal in a criminal case does not bar a claim. Contributory negligence reduces compensation; composite negligence: the claimant can sue any of the joint tortfeasors for the entire amount and the one who pays can recover contribution (Khenyei). Owner's liability: vicarious (the driver is the owner's servant) - also if a vehicle has been sold but registration not transferred, the registered owner remains liable (Pushpa v Shakuntala, 2011: the SC held that 'owner' includes the person in possession after sale - verify).

sections.title: Offences and Penalties (as amended in 2019) and Recent Policy Developments
sections.summary: Known penalty figures appear as numerical MCQs. Treat the figures as 'verify against the bare Act'; some States have varied rates under Sec 200.
key_points: Sec 177: general provision for punishment of offences - fine of Rs 500 (earlier Rs 100); Sec 177A: offences relating to rules of road regulations - Rs 500. Sec 179: disobedience of orders - Rs 2,000; Sec 180: allowing unauthorised persons to drive - Rs 5,000 and/ or imprisonment up to three months; Sec 181: driving without a licence - Rs 5,000; Sec 182: offences relating to licences - Rs 10,000; Sec 183: driving at excessive speed - Rs 1,000 for LMV, Rs 2,000 for medium goods/ passenger vehicles (for a second offence, impounding the licence); Sec 184: DANGEROUS DRIVING - imprisonment up to six months to one year, or fine Rs 1,000-5,000, or both for first offence; subsequent offence within three years: imprisonment up to two years or fine up to Rs 10,000 or both; Sec 185: DRUNKEN DRIVING (blood alcohol content exceeding 30 mg per 100 ml of blood detected through a breath analyser) - first offence: imprisonment up to six months or fine up to Rs 10,000 or both; second or subsequent offence within three years: imprisonment up to two years or fine up to Rs 15,000 or both; Sec 186: driving when mentally or physically unfit - Rs 1,000/ 2,000; Sec 189: racing and trials of speed - imprisonment up to 1 month, fine Rs 5,000, or both; Sec 190: using vehicle in unsafe condition - Rs 1,000; Sec 192: using a vehicle without registration - Rs 5,000 (first), up to Rs 10,000 subsequent; Sec 192A: without permit - up to Rs 10,000; Sec 194: overloading - Rs 20,000 and additional Rs 2,000 per extra tonne; Sec 194B: seat belt - Rs 1,000; Sec 194C: overloading of two-wheelers - Rs 2,000 and disqualification of licence for 3 months; Sec 194D: protective headgear (helmet) violation - Rs 1,000 and disqualification of driving licence for three months; Sec 194E: failure to give way to emergency vehicles - Rs 10,000; Sec 196: driving without insurance - imprisonment up to 3 months or fine Rs 2,000 or both (second offence: 3 months/ Rs 4,000); Sec 199A: OFFENCES BY JUVENILES - where an offence is committed by a juvenile, the guardian or the owner of the motor vehicle shall be deemed to be guilty and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly (imprisonment up to three years and a fine of Rs 25,000); the registration of the motor vehicle shall be cancelled for a period of twelve months; the juvenile shall not be eligible for a driving licence until the age of 25 years (the juvenile is to be tried under the Juvenile Justice Act 2015). Sec 200: compounding of certain offences. The Central Government may notify the maximum fines; States can notify different compounding amounts.

Sec 304A IPC (now Sec 106 BNS): causing death by negligence - imprisonment up to 5 years (2 years for doctors under BNS Sec 106(1) proviso) and fine; hit and run: BNS Sec 106(2) - 10 years' imprisonment + fine for a driver who causes death by rash and negligent driving and escapes without reporting to the police/ magistrate (the provision was kept in abeyance by the Government in January 2024 after protests by transporters until consultations with the All India Motor Transport Congress; verify its current status). Sec 281 BNS: rash driving or riding on a public way - up to 6 months or fine Rs 1,000 or both (formerly Sec 279 IPC).

RECENT POLICY/ CASE DEVELOPMENTS: (1) PM-RAHAT cashless treatment scheme (Rs 1.5 lakh; seven days) and Supreme Court monitoring (May and August 2026); (2) Compensation to Victims (Interim Relief) Scheme, 2026 under Sec 164A - applies to insured vehicles; SC asked for wide publicity (August 2026); (3) LMV/ transport vehicle licence ruling (Mukund Dewangan 2017; reaffirmed by a Constitution Bench in November 2024); (4) Good Samaritan law (Sec 134A) and Save Life Foundation direction (May 2026); (5) Supreme Court's treatment of the MV Act as 'beneficial legislation' for interpretation (liberal construction in favour of victims); (6) Digital enforcement: e-challans, ANPR cameras, DigiLocker documents, Vahan/ Sarathi databases; (7) States' rollback/ modification of penalties under Sec 200; (8) National Road Safety Policy and Bharat NCAP; (9) Aggregator guidelines 2020 (Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines) and Sec 93.

sections.title: Consumer Protection Act 2019: Scheme, Definitions and Consumer Rights
sections.summary: The Consumer Protection Act 2019 (in force from 20 July 2020) replaced the 1986 Act. Core definitions are tested almost every year: consumer, service, defect, deficiency, unfair trade practice, unfair contract.
key_points: Objects: better protection of the interests of consumers; establish authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumer disputes; introduce the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), product liability, mediation and e-commerce regulation. Enacted 2019; the Act and the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 came into force in July 2020.

Sec 2(7) CONSUMER: any person who (i) buys any goods for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment, and includes any user of such goods other than the person who buys such goods for consideration paid or promised, when such use is made with the approval of such person, but does not include a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose; or (ii) hires or avails of any service for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment, and includes any beneficiary of such service other than the person who hires or avails of the services for consideration, when such services are availed of with the approval of the first mentioned person, but does not include a person who avails of such service for any commercial purpose. Explanation: 'commercial purpose' does not include use by a person of goods bought and used by him exclusively for the purpose of earning his livelihood, by means of self-employment; the expressions 'buys any goods' and 'hires or avails any services' include offline or online transactions through electronic means or by teleshopping or direct selling or multi-level marketing.

Laxmi Engineering Works v P.S.G. Industrial Institute (1995): 'commercial purpose' is a question of fact; goods bought for the purpose of generating profit are commercial; the dominant purpose test; goods bought for self-employment are not commercial. Lucknow Development Authority v M.K. Gupta (1994): statutory/ development authorities providing housing and sites are rendering 'service'; compensation for harassment is payable. Indian Medical Association v V.P. Shantha (1995): medical services are 'service' except free services and contracts of personal service; paid-in-part and free-treatment hospitals: the paying patients' services; Spring Meadows Hospital v Harjol Ahluwalia (1998): parents of a minor patient are consumers; Synco Industries v State Bank of Bikaner & Jaipur (2002).

Sec 2(42) SERVICE: service of any description which is made available to potential users and includes, but not limited to, the provision of facilities in connection with banking, financing, insurance, transport, processing, supply of electrical or other energy, telecom, boarding or lodging or both, housing construction, entertainment, amusement or the purveying of news or other information, but does not include the rendering of any service free of charge or under a contract of personal service. Sec 2(10) DEFECT: any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law or undertaken to be performed by a trader in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any goods or product. Sec 2(11) DEFICIENCY: any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law or undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service, and includes any act of negligence or omission or commission by such person which causes loss or injury to the consumer, and the deliberate withholding of relevant information by such person to the consumer.

Sec 2(47) UNFAIR TRADE PRACTICE: a trade practice which, for the purpose of promoting the sale, use or supply of any goods or for the provision of any service, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice including: making false statements/ representations on quality, standard, grade; false or misleading advertisement; not issuing a bill or cash memo or receipt for goods sold or services rendered; refusing to take back or withdraw defective goods or to withdraw or discontinue deficient services and to refund the consideration within the period stipulated in the bill or cash memo, or in the absence of such stipulation, within thirty days; disclosing to other person any personal information given in confidence by the consumer (unless required by law). Sec 2(41) RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICE: a trade practice which tends to bring about manipulation of price or its conditions of delivery or to affect flow of supplies in the market relating to goods or services in such a manner as to impose on the consumers unjustified costs or restrictions, and includes delay beyond the period agreed to by a trader in supply of such goods or in providing the services which has led or is likely to lead to rise in the price; and any trade practice which requires a consumer to buy, hire or avail of any goods or, as the case may be, services as condition precedent to buying, hiring or availing of other goods or services. Sec 2(46) UNFAIR CONTRACT: a contract between a manufacturer or trader or service provider on one hand, and a consumer on the other, having such terms which cause significant change in the rights of such consumer, including: requiring manifestly excessive security deposits; imposing penalty on the consumer, in the event of a breach of contract, which is wholly disproportionate to the loss occurred due to such breach to the other party; refusing to accept early repayment of debts on payment of applicable penalty; entitling a party to terminate the contract unilaterally without reasonable cause; permitting or has the effect of permitting one party to assign the contract to the detriment of the other party who is a consumer, without his consent; imposing on the consumer any unreasonable charge, obligation or condition which puts such consumer to disadvantage. Sec 2(28) MISLEADING ADVERTISEMENT: an advertisement which falsely describes a product or service; or gives a false guarantee to, or is likely to mislead the consumers as to the nature, substance, quantity or quality; or conveys an express or implied representation which, if made by the manufacturer or seller or service provider thereof, would constitute an unfair trade practice; or deliberately conceals important information.

Sec 2(9) CONSUMER RIGHTS (SIX RIGHTS): (i) the right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which are hazardous to life and property; (ii) the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods, products or services, as the case may be, so as to protect the consumer against unfair trade practices; (iii) the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices; (iv) the right to be heard and to be assured that consumer's interests will receive due consideration at appropriate fora; (v) the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers; and (vi) the right to consumer awareness. (Compare with the 8 rights recognised by Consumers International.) Consumer Protection Councils: Central Consumer Protection Council (Sec 3; Minister in charge of Consumer Affairs as Chairperson), State Consumer Protection Councils (Sec 7) and District Consumer Protection Councils (Sec 8) - advisory bodies to promote and protect the rights of the consumer.
