sections.title: Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), Misleading Advertisements and Penalties
sections.summary: New institution under the 2019 Act: class action regulator with powers to recall goods, order refunds and penalise misleading advertisements.
key_points: Sec 10: the Central Government shall establish the CENTRAL CONSUMER PROTECTION AUTHORITY (CCPA) to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of public and consumers, and to promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class. Composition: Chief Commissioner and other Commissioners; investigation wing headed by a Director-General (Sec 15). Sec 18: powers and functions - inquire or cause to be inquired or investigated into violations of consumer rights; file complaints before the appropriate Commission; intervene; review matters relating to safety; issue safety notices; advise on consumer welfare; issue guidelines for prevention of unfair trade practices. Sec 19: power to refer matter for investigation to Director-General; Sec 20: POWER TO RECALL goods and withdraw services, reimburse the prices to purchasers, and discontinue practices which are unfair and prejudicial to consumers' interest; Sec 21: POWER TO ISSUE DIRECTIONS AND PENALTIES AGAINST FALSE OR MISLEADING ADVERTISEMENTS - the CCPA may direct the trader/ manufacturer/ endorser/ advertiser/ publisher to discontinue or modify the advertisement; impose a penalty on a manufacturer or an endorser of up to Rs 10 lakh, and for subsequent contravention up to Rs 50 lakh; prohibit the endorser from making endorsement of any product or service for a period of up to one year, and for subsequent contravention up to three years. Sec 21(4)-(5): an endorser shall not be liable if he exercised due diligence to verify the veracity of the claims made in the advertisement. Sec 22: search and seizure; Sec 24: appeal against CCPA orders to the National Commission within 30 days. Sec 17: complaints to the CCPA.

Sec 88: PENALTY for non-compliance of directions of the Central Authority - imprisonment up to six months or fine up to Rs 20 lakh or both. Sec 89: PUNISHMENT FOR FALSE OR MISLEADING ADVERTISEMENT - imprisonment up to two years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh; for every subsequent offence - imprisonment up to five years and fine up to Rs 50 lakh. Sec 90: punishment for manufacturing for sale or storing, selling or distributing or importing products containing adulterant - imprisonment up to six months and fine up to Rs 1 lakh (where no injury); injury - up to one year and Rs 3 lakh; grievous hurt - up to seven years and Rs 5 lakh; death - not less than 7 years extendable to life and fine not less than Rs 10 lakh. Sec 91: punishment for manufacturing for sale or storing, selling or distributing or importing spurious goods - similar graded punishment. (Figures are indicative - verify the bare Act.) Sec 92: cognizance of offences by courts (Magistrate).

SUBORDINATE INSTRUMENTS (HOT): Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 - apply to all goods and services bought or sold over digital or electronic network, including digital products; to all models of e-commerce (marketplace e-commerce entity and inventory e-commerce entity), to e-commerce retail, and to all forms of unfair trade practices across all models; duties: appoint a grievance officer (acknowledge within 48 hours; redress within one month), no unfair prices (cannot manipulate price), no discrimination, display of seller details, country of origin, return/ refund/ warranty information; no cancellation charges unless similar charges are borne by the e-commerce entity; no flash sales that manipulate the market (Rule 5). Consumer Protection (Direct Selling) Rules 2021. Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns 2023 (notified 30 November 2023; 13 specified dark patterns: false urgency, basket sneaking, confirm shaming, forced action, subscription trap, interface interference, bait and switch, drip pricing, disguised advertisements, nagging, trick question, SaaS billing, rogue malwares). Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements 2022 (9 June 2022; conditions for valid advertisements; due diligence; duties of manufacturers/ service providers, advertisers and advertising agencies; surrogate and bait advertisements; free claims; endorsements by celebrities require due diligence and disclosures). Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Greenwashing or Misleading Environmental Claims 2024.

sections.title: Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions: Composition, Jurisdiction, Procedure and Appeals
sections.summary: Pecuniary jurisdiction, limitation, timelines, appeals and pre-deposit are standard numerical questions.
key_points: THREE-TIER STRUCTURE: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (District Commission, Sec 28), State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (State Commission, Sec 42), National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (National Commission, Sec 53). The District Commission consists of a President and not less than two other members (one of whom is a woman). State Commission: a President (a person who is or has been a Judge of a High Court) and not less than four members (maximum as prescribed); National Commission: President (a person who is or has been a Judge of the Supreme Court) and not less than four and not more than such number of members as may be prescribed (up to 11). The 'Consumer Protection (Qualification for Appointment, Method of Recruitment, Procedure of Appointment, Term of Office, Resignation and Removal of the President and Members of the State Commission and District Commission) Rules, 2020' prescribe conditions; Selection Committees - the Supreme Court in various orders (including in 2024) directed adherence to the Rules.

PECUNIARY JURISDICTION (Sec 34, 47, 58 as amended by the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 notified on 30 December 2021): the value of the goods or services PAID AS CONSIDERATION decides jurisdiction: District Commission - up to Rs 50 lakh; State Commission - more than Rs 50 lakh but not more than Rs 2 crore; National Commission - more than Rs 2 crore. (Under the original 2019 Act, the District's limit was Rs 1 crore and the State's Rs 10 crore - these were on the basis of value of goods/ services AND compensation claimed under the 1986 Act; the 2019 Act changed the basis to the consideration paid.) Rutu Mihir Panchal v Union of India (2025 INSC 593, decided 29 April 2025): the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the pecuniary jurisdiction provisions based on the value of consideration paid and the 2021 Rules, rejecting the challenge that the change was arbitrary; it observed that Parliament is free to prescribe jurisdiction and that the 2021 Rules were validly made. In 2026 the Supreme Court has again noted anomalies in the consideration-based approach (for example, cases where the consideration paid is small but the loss/ claim is large, as in hospital or insurance cases) and sought the Centre's response; the legislative/ rule position may change - verify.

TERRITORIAL JURISDICTION (Sec 34(2)): a complaint may be instituted in a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction (a) the opposite party or each of the opposite parties, where there are more than one, at the time of the institution of the complaint, ordinarily resides or carries on business or has a branch office or personally works for gain; or (b) any of the opposite parties, where there are more than one, at the time of the institution of the complaint, actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business or has a branch office, or personally works for gain, provided that in such case either the permission of the District Commission is given, or the opposite parties who do not reside, or carry on business or have a branch office, or personally work for gain, as the case may be, acquiesce in such institution; or (c) the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises; or (d) the complainant resides or personally works for gain (NEW in 2019 - convenient forum for the consumer).

WHO MAY FILE (Sec 35(1)): (a) the consumer to whom such goods are sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered, or such service is provided or agreed to be provided; (b) any recognised consumer association, whether the consumer is a member or not; (c) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest, with the permission of the District Commission, on behalf of or for the benefit of all consumers so interested (class action/ representative complaint); (d) the Central Government, the Central Authority or the State Government; (e) in case of death of a consumer, his legal heir or representative; or (f) in case of a consumer being a minor, his parent or legal guardian. Complaints can be filed ELECTRONICALLY (e-Daakhil/ e-Jagriti portal), by post or in person. Fee: nil for complaints up to Rs 5 lakh; graded fee beyond (Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules 2020).

LIMITATION (Sec 69): the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within TWO YEARS from the date on which the cause of action has arisen; a complaint may be entertained after the period specified if the complainant satisfies the Commission that he had sufficient cause for not filing the complaint within such period (the Commission must record reasons for condoning delay). Continuing wrong: fresh cause of action.

PROCEDURE (Secs 35-38): admissibility of complaint to be decided within 21 days from the date of filing (Sec 36(3)); if the question of admissibility is not decided within 21 days, the complaint shall be deemed to have been admitted; the opposite party must be given a notice and shall give his version within 30 days, extendable by not more than 15 days (Sec 38(2)(a)) - the Supreme Court in New India Assurance v Hilli Multipurpose Cold Storage (2020, Constitution Bench) held that the 45-day limit is mandatory and the Commission has no power to extend beyond 45 days; where the opposite party denies or disputes the allegations that need not be tested by laboratory, the Commission decides on the basis of evidence/ affidavits (documents); Sec 38(7): the complaint shall be decided as expeditiously as possible and endeavour shall be made to decide the complaint within a period of THREE MONTHS from the date of receipt of notice by opposite party where the complaint does not require analysis or testing of commodities and within FIVE MONTHS if it requires analysis or testing. The Commission has the powers of a civil court under the CPC (summoning, discovery, affidavits, commissions) - Sec 38(9); the proceedings are judicial proceedings (Sec 38(10)). Sec 37: MEDIATION - at the first hearing, if it appears to the District Commission that there exists elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, it may, at the option of the parties, direct them to give their consent in writing to refer the matter for settlement by mediation (Mediation cells attached to Commissions - Secs 74-81).

RELIEFS (Sec 39): remove the defect pointed out by the appropriate laboratory; replace the goods with new goods of similar description which shall be free from any defect; return to the complainant the price or the charges paid; pay such amount as may be awarded as compensation for any loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the negligence of the opposite party (and PUNITIVE DAMAGES in appropriate circumstances); provide for adequate costs to parties; direct the opposite party to discontinue the unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practice or not to repeat them; not to offer the hazardous or unsafe goods for sale; withdraw the hazardous goods from being offered for sale; cease manufacture of hazardous goods; issue corrective advertisement to neutralise the effect of misleading advertisement; to pay such sum as determined if it is of the opinion that loss or injury has been suffered by a large number of consumers who are not identifiable conveniently (not less than 5% of the value of such defective goods sold or service provided, to be credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund). Sec 40: POWER OF REVIEW - the District Commission shall have the power to review any of the order passed by it if there is an error apparent on the face of the record, either of its own motion or on an application made by any of the parties within thirty days of such order.

APPEALS: Sec 41 - from the District Commission to the State Commission within 45 days (may be entertained after 45 days for sufficient cause); no appeal shall be entertained by the State Commission unless the appellant has deposited FIFTY PER CENT of the amount ordered by the District Commission. Sec 51 - from the State Commission (in its original jurisdiction) to the National Commission within 30 days; with the deposit of 50% of the amount. Sec 67 - from the National Commission (in its original jurisdiction) to the Supreme Court within 30 days (the Supreme Court may entertain after 30 days for sufficient cause). Also: appeals from the CCPA to the National Commission (Sec 24). Second appeal: revision petitions before the National Commission against State Commission's appellate orders (Sec 58(1)(b)): Revision lies where the State Commission appears to have exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it, or failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested in it, or acted illegally or with material irregularity. No second appeal lies against the State Commission's appellate order; revision lies to the National Commission under Sec 58(1)(b), and the Supreme Court may be approached under Art 136.

ENFORCEMENT (Secs 71-72): Sec 71: every order made by a District Commission, State Commission or the National Commission shall be enforced by it in the same manner as if it were a decree made by a Court in a suit before it and the provisions of Order XXI of the CPC shall apply, as far as may be, subject to the modification that every reference therein to the decree shall be construed as reference to the order made under this Act. Sec 72: PENALTY FOR NON-COMPLIANCE of the order - imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one month but which may extend to three years, or a fine which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees but which may extend to one lakh rupees, or both; the Commission has the powers of the Judicial Magistrate of the First Class for the purpose of trial of such offences (Sec 72(2)); the offences may be tried summarily (Sec 72(3)).

INTERIM ORDERS and special powers: The Commission may issue interim orders; National Commission has power to hear cases against unfair contracts (Sec 59(2)); State Commission - Sec 49(2): declare any terms of contract which is unfair to any consumer to be null and void. Hearings may be conducted by video conferencing under the Rules. Review powers: State/ National Commissions (Sec 50, Sec 60).

sections.title: Product Liability, Unfair Contracts and Key Case Law
sections.summary: Product liability is a new, examiner-friendly chapter of the 2019 Act. Combine with medical negligence and builder-buyer case law.
key_points: Chapter VI (Secs 82-87) PRODUCT LIABILITY: Sec 82: a product liability action may be brought by a complainant for any harm caused by a defective product manufactured by a product manufacturer or serviced by a product service provider or sold by a product seller. 'Harm' includes damage to any property other than the product itself, personal injury, illness or death, mental agony or emotional distress attendant to personal injury or illness or damage to property, and any loss of consortium or services or other loss resulting from a harm; it does not include any harm caused to a product itself or any damage to property on account of breach of warranty conditions or any commercial or economic loss, including any direct or consequential loss relating thereto. Sec 84: LIABILITY OF PRODUCT MANUFACTURERS - a product manufacturer shall be liable in a product liability action, if (a) the product contains a manufacturing defect; or (b) the product is defective in design; or (c) there is a deviation from manufacturing specifications; or (d) the product does not conform to the express warranty; or (e) the product fails to contain adequate instructions of correct usage to prevent any harm or any warning regarding improper or incorrect usage. Sec 85: product service provider liable where the service was faulty, imperfect, deficient or inadequate in quality, nature or manner of performance; or there was an act of omission, commission, negligence or conscious withholding of information which caused harm; or the service provider did not issue adequate cautions or instructions; or the service did not conform to express warranty or the terms and conditions of the contract. Sec 86: product seller (who is not a product manufacturer) liable if he has exercised substantial control over designing, testing, manufacturing, packaging or labelling; or altered or modified the product; or made an express warranty independent of the manufacturer; or the product has been sold and the identity of the product manufacturer is not known or the manufacturer is not subject to Indian law / cannot be enforced; or failed to exercise reasonable care in assembling, inspecting or maintaining; or failed to pass on a warning or instruction. Sec 87: EXCEPTIONS - a product manufacturer shall not be liable if at the time of harm the product was misused, altered or modified; sale by a seller is covered under conditions; a warning was given; the harm was caused to a user who was under the influence of alcohol or drugs not prescribed; the product is sold to an experienced user/ in bulk to another manufacturer where the buyer is a sophisticated user with knowledge; etc.

UNFAIR CONTRACTS: State Commission (Sec 49(2)) and National Commission (Sec 59(2)) have the power to declare any terms of contract which is unfair to any consumer to be null and void (if complaints are within their jurisdiction). The Supreme Court in Pioneer Urban Land v Govindan Raghavan (2019) and related decisions held that one-sided builder-buyer agreements (e.g., clauses allowing forfeiture of heavy sums for buyer's default while paying negligible compensation for the builder's delay) are unfair trade practices and not binding; buyers entitled to refund with interest when possession is inordinately delayed (Wg Cdr Arifur Rahman Khan v DLF Southern Homes, 2020; Experion Developers v Sushma Ashok Shiroor, 2022).

MEDIATION (Secs 74-81): Consumer Mediation Cells attached to the District, State and National Commissions; mediation by empanelled mediators; settlement agreement signed by the parties; order of the Commission to give effect; no appeal against orders passed with consent. ARBITRATION CLAUSE: a consumer complaint is not barred by an arbitration agreement - the CPA remedy is an additional statutory remedy (Emaar MGF Land v Aftab Singh, 2018, relying on the 1986 Act and Sec 100 of the CPA 2019; the decision has been reaffirmed). RERA and the CPA are concurrent remedies (Imperia Structures v Anil Patni, 2020). Insurance/ banking, telecom and similar services also under the Act, subject to other statutory forums where the law says so (e.g., Telecom: Sec 7B of the Telegraph Act arbitration was held not to bar consumer forum in the Supreme Court's decision in General Manager Telecom v M. Krishnan, 2009 - the Court held that Sec 7B Telegraph Act made the arbitration route the exclusive remedy for telephone billing disputes; verify current position after the 2019 Act and the Telecommunications Act 2023).

MEDICAL AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICES: Medical negligence cases - Bolam standard and Jacob Mathew; V. Kishan Rao v Nikhil Super Speciality Hospital (2010) held that expert evidence isn't mandatory in each case. Advocates: the Supreme Court in Bar of Indian Lawyers v D.K. Gandhi PS National Institute of Communicable Diseases (14 May 2024) held that advocates' services under a contract of personal service/ professional services are not 'service' under the CPA 2019; the decision was later stayed/ taken up in a review and referred to a larger Bench (verify the current status); earlier, Dr. Jacob Mathew. Banking and insurance services: 'service' under Sec 2(42); Insurance: the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority; the Ombudsman scheme; claims repudiation without valid ground is deficiency.

SUPREME COURT CASE SNAPSHOT: Lucknow Development Authority v M.K. Gupta (1994); Laxmi Engineering Works v P.S.G. (1995); IMA v V.P. Shantha (1995); Spring Meadows Hospital v Harjol Ahluwalia (1998); State of Karnataka v Vishwabharathi House Building Co-op Society (2003) (validity of the Act); Pioneer Urban Land v Govindan Raghavan (2019); Imperia Structures v Anil Patni (2020); New India Assurance v Hilli Multipurpose Cold Storage (2020); Rutu Mihir Panchal v UoI (2025).
common_traps: Product liability covers manufacturers, service providers and sellers (Secs 84-86); 'harm' excludes damage to the product itself and purely commercial loss.
Arbitration clause doesn't oust the consumer forum.
Unfair contract declarations are by State/ National Commissions.
likely_questions: Product liability is dealt with in: Chapter VI (Secs 82-87).
Sec 84 liability of: product manufacturer.
Does an arbitration clause bar a consumer complaint? No.

sections.title: Nature, Scope and Foundations: Rule of Law and Separation of Powers
sections.summary: Conceptual base for 3 questions: definition, Dicey's rule of law, droit administratif, separation of powers in India.
key_points: Administrative law is the law relating to the powers and procedures of administrative agencies, including the law governing judicial review of administrative action (Ivor Jennings: the law relating to administration; K.C. Davis: the law concerning the powers and procedures of administrative agencies, including especially the law governing judicial review of administrative action). In India it has grown from the common law of judicial review, Arts 12-14, 32, 226, 300, 311, and statutes (tribunals, RTI, Lokpal). Administrative functions are classified as rule-making (legislative), rule-adjudication (judicial/ quasi-judicial), rule-application (executive/ administrative) and ministerial.

RULE OF LAW (A.V. Dicey, 'Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution'): three meanings - (1) supremacy of regular law as opposed to arbitrary power; (2) equality before the law; (3) the constitution is the result of ordinary law of the land (rights flow from judicial decisions). Indian position: the rule of law is part of the basic structure (Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain, 1975); Art 14 prohibits arbitrariness (E.P. Royappa v State of Tamil Nadu, 1974: equality is antithetic to arbitrariness; Maneka Gandhi v Union of India, 1978: any action must be just, fair and reasonable). Shayara Bano (2017) applied manifest arbitrariness to legislation. ADM Jabalpur v Shivkant Shukla (1976) (Habeas Corpus case) was overruled by K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

DROIT ADMINISTRATIF (French administrative law): a separate body of public law applied by the Conseil d'Etat administrative courts to disputes involving the administration; Dicey criticised it as inconsistent with the rule of law; in India the ordinary courts review administrative action; administrative tribunals are subject to constitutional courts (L. Chandra Kumar). Position of the administrative law in USA: Administrative Procedure Act 1946.

SEPARATION OF POWERS: not rigidly followed in India (Ram Jawaya Kapur v State of Punjab, 1955: the Indian Constitution has not recognised the doctrine of separation of powers in its absolute rigidity but the functions of the different parts or branches of the Government have been sufficiently differentiated); Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain: separation of powers is part of the basic structure; Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973): basic structure doctrine; Delegation, tribunals and the administrative adjudication are accommodated within the framework; In re Delhi Laws Act (1951). Judicial review is itself a basic feature (L. Chandra Kumar; Minerva Mills v Union of India, 1980).

Sources of administrative law: Constitution; statutes (e.g., Administrative Tribunals Act 1985, RTI Act 2005, CVC Act 2003, Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013, Commissions of Inquiry Act 1952); delegated legislation; administrative directions/ circulars (binding only in some cases - Union of India v Azadi Bachao Andolan (2003): circulars issued by CBDT under statutory power binding on tax authorities); judicial decisions.

'STATE' under Art 12 and public law remedies: 'authority' includes Government, Parliament, State legislatures, local authorities and 'other authorities' (Ramana Dayaram Shetty v International Airport Authority, 1979 - instrumentality test; Ajay Hasia v Khalid Mujib, 1981 - tests for an instrumentality or agency of the State; Pradeep Kumar Biswas v Indian Institute of Chemical Biology, 2002 - 'financial, functional and administrative domination'; Zee Telefilms v Union of India (2005)). Writ jurisdiction under Art 226 extends to 'any person or authority' discharging public functions (Andi Mukta Sadguru v V.R. Rudani, 1989; K.K. Saksena v International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage, 2015; Federal Bank v Sagar Thomas, 2003).

sections.title: Delegated Legislation
sections.summary: Constitutional limits on delegation, 'essential legislative function', conditional legislation, sub-delegation and control. Frequently asked.
key_points: Delegated legislation = law made by an executive authority under power delegated by the Legislature. Forms: rules, regulations, bye-laws, orders, notifications, schemes. Reasons: pressure on parliamentary time, technicality, flexibility, emergencies, experimentation. DELEGATUS NON POTEST DELEGARE: a delegate cannot further delegate (sub-delegation requires express or implied authority).

CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITS: Legislature can delegate but cannot abdicate. IN RE DELHI LAWS ACT (1951, Special Reference 1 of 1951): the Supreme Court (7-judge bench, separate opinions) held that the Legislature may delegate ancillary or subsidiary powers but cannot delegate its ESSENTIAL LEGISLATIVE FUNCTION (laying down the legislative policy and enacting it as a binding rule); power to repeal or modify laws ('Henry VIII clause') beyond limited extent is excessive; conditional legislation is valid. Harishankar Bagla v State of Madhya Pradesh (1954): essential legislative function consists in the determination or choosing of the legislative policy and of formally enacting that policy into a binding rule of conduct; the legislature must declare the policy and lay down the standard; delegation is valid if policy is laid down; Hamdard Dawakhana v Union of India (1960): the Legislature cannot leave to the executive the decision on what constitutes a 'disease' or what is an objectionable advertisement - delegation was excessive as the Act (Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act 1954) left the central government to add diseases without any guidance; Vasu Dev Singh v Union of India (2006); Gwalior Rayon Silk Mfg v Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax (1974): power to fix rate of tax by the Government valid if guidelines exist; Municipal Corporation of Delhi v Birla Cotton Spinning and Weaving Mills (1968): taxation power - essential legislative function includes the imposition of tax; the delegation of power to fix rate within limits is valid; Devi Das Gopal Krishnan v State of Punjab (1967): excessive delegation to fix tax rate struck.

CONDITIONAL LEGISLATION vs DELEGATED LEGISLATION: in conditional legislation the Legislature makes the law complete and leaves to the executive the determination of the time/ place/ manner/ fulfilment of a condition for bringing it into operation (Queen v Burah, 1878 PC: power to determine the area to which the Act applies is conditional legislation; the Indian legislature is not a delegate of the British Parliament; Rajnarain Singh v Chairman, Patna Administration Committee, 1954: the Legislature cannot delegate power to modify essential provisions). In delegated legislation, the delegate frames subsidiary rules and has some law-making discretion. Cases: Sardar Inder Singh v State of Rajasthan (1957); Hamdard; Registrar of Co-operative Societies v K. Kunjabmu (1980).

CLASSIFICATION: by delegator - parent Act; by purpose - supplementary, contingent, ancillary; by nature - enabling, extending, modifying (Henry VIII clause: authorises the executive to amend the statute itself), exemption, taxation, commencement; by authority - sub-delegated legislation (e.g., rules by Government, bye-laws by local authorities, orders by Commissioner). Judicial notice: delegated legislation made by the Central Government is judicially noticed.

CONTROL OF DELEGATED LEGISLATION: (A) JUDICIAL CONTROL - (1) SUBSTANTIVE ULTRA VIRES: the rule is beyond the scope of the parent Act or violates the Constitution (fundamental rights) or repugnant to the parent Act or unreasonable; (2) PROCEDURAL ULTRA VIRES: failure to follow the prescribed procedure (consultation, publication; Raza Buland Sugar Co v Municipal Board Rampur (1965): failure to follow the prescribed procedure makes the bye-law invalid); (3) UNREASONABLENESS: Kruse v Johnson (1898): bye-laws made by local authorities may be struck down if they are manifestly unjust, oppressive or partial; Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt Ltd v Union of India (1985): subordinate legislation can be challenged on grounds applicable to ordinary executive action and also on grounds of arbitrariness, unreasonableness and violation of Art 14 (and that subordinate legislation is not shielded by a presumption of constitutionality enjoyed by plenary legislation); State of Tamil Nadu v P. Krishnamurthy (2006): the grounds on which delegated legislation can be challenged: lack of legislative competence; violating the parent Act; violating Constitution; and arbitrariness/ unreasonableness in the narrow sense - an unreasonable bye-law may be struck down only if it is 'manifestly arbitrary'; Cellular Operators Association of India v TRAI (2003). (B) LEGISLATIVE/ PARLIAMENTARY CONTROL: laying of rules before the House (whether laying is mandatory or directory depends on the statute - Atlas Cycle Industries v State of Haryana (1979) treated it as directory in that case); Committees on Subordinate Legislation (Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha); scrutiny; the power of the Houses to annul; (C) PUBLICATION: delegated legislation must be published (Harla v State of Rajasthan, 1951: laws must be published in the official Gazette/ made known to the people before becoming effective). (D) CONSULTATION with affected interests and pre-publication of drafts.

SUB-DELEGATION: allowed only if the parent Act authorises it expressly or by necessary implication (Ganpati Sitaram Balvalkar v Waman Shripad Mage, 1981; Sahni Silk Mills v ESIC, 1994: power to sub-delegate must be conferred). Henry VIII clauses are viewed with suspicion; Court may read them down.

ORDINANCES (Art 123/ 213) and EMERGENCY regulations: executive legislative power, subject to approval; not delegated legislation in the strict sense but similar; Krishna Kumar Singh v State of Bihar (2017): re-promulgation of ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution. ADMINISTRATIVE DIRECTIONS: circulars, guidelines, manuals - non-statutory, binding on subordinate officers only; courts apply them if they fill gaps and do not conflict with law; Union of India v Azadi Bachao Andolan (2003): circular in tax context; State of UP v Chandra Prakash Pandey (2001).

sections.title: Judicial Review of Administrative Action; Discretion; Legitimate Expectation; Proportionality
sections.summary: Grounds (illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety, proportionality), abuse of discretion, legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel.
key_points: SOURCE: Art 32 (Supreme Court - enforcement of fundamental rights; itself a fundamental right) and Art 226 (High Courts - any person or authority, for enforcement of fundamental rights and 'for any other purpose'), Art 227 (superintendence over subordinate courts and tribunals), Art 136 (special leave), Art 142. Judicial review is part of the basic structure (L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India, 1997).

GROUNDS - Lord Diplock in Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service (GCHQ case, 1985): (1) ILLEGALITY - the decision-maker must correctly understand the law and give effect to it (acting ultra vires, error of law, delegation/ dictation, fettering of discretion, irrelevant considerations, improper purposes, non-application of mind); (2) IRRATIONALITY (Wednesbury unreasonableness) - a decision so outrageous in its defiance of logic or of accepted moral standards that no sensible person who had applied his mind to the question could have arrived at it; (3) PROCEDURAL IMPROPRIETY - failure to observe basic rules of natural justice or procedural fairness or statutory procedure; and (4) PROPORTIONALITY (a further ground that Lord Diplock foresaw). Associated Provincial Picture Houses v Wednesbury Corporation (1948): the court can interfere only if the authority took into account irrelevant considerations or ignored relevant ones, or reached a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it.

ABUSE OF DISCRETION: (a) improper purpose (Sharp v Wakefield; Padfield v Minister of Agriculture, 1968 - discretion must be exercised to promote the policy and objects of the Act; Barium Chemicals Ltd v Company Law Board, 1967 - subjective satisfaction is reviewable if there are no material facts); (b) mala fides (State of Punjab v Gurdial Singh, 1980: mala fide exercise of power for acquiring land; S. Pratap Singh v State of Punjab, 1964); (c) irrelevant considerations/ ignoring relevant ones (Rohtas Industries v S.D. Agarwal, 1969); (d) non-application of mind/ acting under dictation (Commissioner of Police v Gordhandas Bhanji, 1952: order issued under dictation of a Minister invalid); (e) fettering of discretion by rigid policies (British Oxygen Co v Board of Trade); (f) unreasonableness/ arbitrariness (Maneka Gandhi; Shrilekha Vidyarthi v State of UP, 1991: arbitrary termination of government counsel - Art 14 applies to government contractual and appointment decisions); (g) unstructured discretion violates Art 14 (State of West Bengal v Anwar Ali Sarkar, 1952; Maneka Gandhi: power of impounding passport without guidelines). Subjective satisfaction: where the statute says 'if the authority is satisfied' or 'in the opinion of the authority', courts still examine whether the opinion was formed on relevant material.

PROPORTIONALITY: whether the means used are suitably related and no more than necessary to achieve the aim (R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Daly, 2001). India: Om Kumar v Union of India (2001): proportionality applies strictly to cases involving fundamental rights, while the Wednesbury standard applies to other administrative decisions; Ranjit Thakur v Union of India (1987): punishment so disproportionate as to shock the conscience of the court is open to judicial review (court-martial); Union of India v G. Ganayutham (1997): the proportionality principle in administrative law; Modern Dental College v State of MP (2016) and K.S. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar, 2018) adopted the four-prong proportionality test (legitimate aim; rational connection; necessity/ least restrictive alternative; balancing); Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020): restrictions on the internet must satisfy proportionality; Chairman, All India Railway Rec. Board v K. Shyam Kumar (2010): 'Wednesbury' and proportionality.

JUDICIAL REVIEW IN CONTRACTS AND TENDERS: Tata Cellular v Union of India (1994): judicial review of administrative action in tenders is limited to the decision-making process, not the decision; the Government may choose the contractor; the Court examines whether there was illegality, irrationality or procedural impropriety; Jagdish Mandal v State of Orissa (2007): two tests - whether the process or the decision is mala fide/ intended to favour someone, and whether the process is so arbitrary and irrational that no responsible authority could have reached it; Michigan Rubber v State of Karnataka (2012); Air India Ltd v Cochin International Airport (2000). Art 14 applies to government contracts (Ramana Dayaram Shetty).

LEGITIMATE EXPECTATION: a person may have a legitimate expectation of being treated in a certain way by an administrative authority due to a promise, representation, or a consistent past practice (Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister, 1985; Attorney General for Hong Kong v Ng Yuen Shiu, 1983). Procedural legitimate expectation (a right to a hearing/ consultation) is recognised; substantive legitimate expectation (a substantive benefit) is recognised in India with limits. Indian cases: Navjyoti Co-operative Group Housing Society v Union of India (1992): legitimate expectation of consideration in seniority-based allotment; Food Corporation of India v Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries (1993): fair play; a legitimate expectation is not a right - it's a ground for judicial review; Punjab Communications Ltd v Union of India (1999): changes of policy can defeat a legitimate expectation if it's based on public interest and the change is not arbitrary; Union of India v Hindustan Development Corporation (1993); Jitendra Kumar v State of Haryana (2008): legitimate expectation cannot be claimed against a statutory provision; Sethi Auto Service Station v DDA (2009): the doctrine is not an independent substantive right but a ground; Official Liquidator v Dayanand (2008); Hira Tikkoo v Union Territory of Chandigarh (2004). The doctrine is a part of Art 14 and rule of law.

PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL IN PUBLIC LAW: Central London Property Trust v High Trees House (1947); Indian: Union of India v Indo-Afghan Agencies (1968): the Government is bound by its representation if the other party has acted to its detriment (altered position); Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v State of UP (1979): no need to show detriment - only alteration of position; the doctrine is applicable against the Government, even in exercise of governmental functions, but it cannot be invoked to compel the Government to act contrary to law, or to the detriment of public interest (public interest overrides - e.g., when a policy changes in public interest the court weighs). Doctrine of estoppel does not apply against the legislature; Union of India v Anglo Afghan Agencies. Contrast with legitimate expectation (legitimate expectation does not need a promise and doesn't give a right of enforcement).

REASONED DECISIONS: duty to give reasons is a rule of natural justice and a fundamental of good administration: Siemens Engineering and Manufacturing Co v Union of India (1976) (quasi-judicial orders must be reasoned); Maneka Gandhi; S.N. Mukherjee v Union of India (1990): reasons must be recorded in administrative orders where required by law and for appellate/ revisional review; Mohinder Singh Gill v Chief Election Commissioner (1978): public orders publicly made, in exercise of a statutory power, must be judged by the objective texts or the reasons contained in them and cannot be supplemented by fresh reasons in the shape of affidavit or otherwise. Judicial review of policy decisions: courts do not interfere with policy unless arbitrary, mala fide or violate fundamental rights (Balco Employees Union v Union of India, 2002; State of Madhya Pradesh v Narmada Bachao Andolan, 2011). 'Fair play in action' and bias in selection.

sections.title: Principles of Natural Justice
sections.summary: Audi alteram partem, nemo judex in causa sua, reasoned decisions, exceptions and post-decisional hearing; Maneka Gandhi and A.K. Kraipak are must-know.
key_points: Natural justice = fairness in procedure, implicit in Art 14 and Art 21 (Maneka Gandhi v Union of India, 1978: natural justice is part of Art 21's 'procedure established by law'; the 'procedure' must be fair, just and reasonable). A.K. Kraipak v Union of India (1969): the dividing line between administrative and quasi-judicial functions has become thin and is being gradually obliterated; natural justice principles apply to administrative actions that affect rights/ civil consequences; also a selection board member who was a candidate sat in the selection - bias. Ridge v Baldwin (1964): natural justice applies to administrative dismissal; Cooper v Wandsworth Board of Works (1863): even where the statute is silent, the right to hearing is implied ('the justice of the common law will supply the omission of the legislature'); State of Orissa v Dr (Miss) Binapani Dei (1967): where an order has civil consequences, an opportunity to be heard must be given; Swadeshi Cotton Mills v Union of India (1981): even in cases of exigency, a post-decisional hearing may be provided; Maneka Gandhi: post-decisional hearing is permissible in urgent cases (impounding of passport).

TWO RULES: (1) NEMO JUDEX IN CAUSA SUA - no man shall be a judge in his own cause (rule against bias). Types of bias: (a) PECUNIARY BIAS - even a small pecuniary interest disqualifies (Dr. Bonham's case, 1610; Dimes v Grand Junction Canal, 1852 - Lord Chancellor held shares in the company; decree set aside; Jeejeebhoy v Assistant Collector, Thana (1965): the disqualification applies to a pecuniary interest); (b) PERSONAL BIAS - hostility, friendship, relationship (Mineral Development Ltd v State of Bihar, 1960; A.K. Kraipak); (c) SUBJECT-MATTER BIAS - a direct interest in the subject matter or the policy - not ordinary (Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v Andhra Pradesh SRTC, 1959: the Secretary who heard objections was the one who proposed the scheme - disqualified; the Minister's role - departmental bias); (d) OFFICIAL/ DEPARTMENTAL BIAS (R v Sussex Justices ex p McCarthy, 1924: 'it is not merely of some importance but is of fundamental importance that justice should not only be done, but should manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done'); (e) PREJUDGMENT. TEST: 'REAL LIKELIHOOD OF BIAS' vs 'REASONABLE SUSPICION' - Indian courts follow the real likelihood test (Manak Lal v Dr Prem Chand Singhvi, 1957; S. Parthasarathi v State of Andhra Pradesh, 1973: the test is whether a reasonable man would think there was a likelihood of bias; Ranjit Thakur v Union of India, 1987: bias of a commanding officer who was the complainant and the judge; Rattan Lal Sharma v Managing Committee Dr Hari Ram Co-ed Higher Secondary School, 1993). In India the 'reasonable apprehension of bias' test is applied; the actual proof of bias is not necessary. DOCTRINE OF NECESSITY: a biased authority may act if no other authority is competent (Election Commission of India v Dr. Subramaniam Swamy, 1996; Ashok Kumar Yadav v State of Haryana, 1985 - members of the Public Service Commission who had relatives among candidates must withdraw).

(2) AUDI ALTERAM PARTEM - hear the other side: elements - (a) NOTICE: adequate, clear, stating the grounds/ charges (Kanda v Government of Malaya); Canara Bank v Debasis Das (2003): natural justice: notice, an opportunity to explain, impartial, reasoned order; (b) DISCLOSURE of materials relied on - Kanungo & Co v Collector of Customs (1972): disclosure of the material relied upon and the right to cross-examine is part of a fair hearing; Hira Nath Mishra v Principal, Rajendra Medical College (1973): in-camera enquiry - a fair hearing - cross-examination can be dispensed with if the witnesses fear victimisation and the substance of evidence is disclosed; (c) HEARING - oral hearing is not always required - written representation may suffice (Union of India v J.P. Mitter, 1971); (d) CROSS-EXAMINATION and legal representation are not necessary in every case (J.K. Aggarwal v Haryana Seeds Development Corporation, 1991; Board of Trustees of Port of Bombay v Dilip Kumar Raghavendranath Nadkarni, 1983: a right to representation by a lawyer is not absolute - fairness where the employer is represented by a legally trained person); (e) REASONED DECISION; (f) EVIDENCE.

'USELESS FORMALITY' / PREJUDICE THEORY: S.L. Kapoor v Jagmohan (1980): where the facts are admitted or undisputed and only one conclusion is possible, a hearing may be dispensed with as it would be a useless formality; M.C. Mehta v Union of India (1999); State of UP v Sudhir Kumar Singh (2020): the Supreme Court summarised that the violation of natural justice must cause prejudice to the aggrieved - 'prejudice' must be demonstrated; in the case of procedural violations the courts examine whether the omitted procedure would have made any difference. Contrasting view: in cases of denial of a hearing, the order is void ab initio (Nawabkhan Abbaskhan v State of Gujarat, 1974 - prejudice need not be shown where natural justice is breached in a fundamental way).

EXCLUSION/ EXCEPTIONS: (1) by statute (but any such exclusion must be reasonable - Art 14 and 21); (2) emergency/ urgency (a post-decisional hearing: Maneka Gandhi; Liberty Oil Mills v Union of India, 1984); (3) legislative acts/ general policy (no hearing required for legislative action - Union of India v Cynamide India Ltd, 1987); (4) impracticability (mass cases); (5) confidentiality/ national security (Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister - national security exception); (6) academic judgments (Maharashtra State Board of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education v K.S. Gandhi, 1991: a hearing is not required to disqualify a candidate for copying where the examination authorities followed the process; Jawaharlal Nehru University v B.S. Narwal, 1980); (7) preliminary investigations (no hearing at the stage of a preliminary inquiry; but a show cause is needed at final stage - Union of India v W.N. Chadha, 1993: no hearing at the stage of investigation to issue letters rogatory); (8) 'no prejudice'.

Specific contexts: (i) Departmental inquiry - Art 311(2): reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of charges; exceptions in the second proviso (Union of India v Tulsiram Patel, 1985: the Court upheld the second proviso clauses (a), (b) and (c) - dismissal without inquiry when the conduct led to conviction on a criminal charge; where it's not reasonably practicable to hold an inquiry; or in the interest of the security of the State - but the reasons must be recorded and the order is subject to judicial review). (ii) Termination of employment of probationers or temporary employees: if the termination is a punishment (stigma), enquiry required (Parshotam Lal Dhingra v Union of India, 1958 - tests: whether the servant has a right to the post and whether the order involves evil consequences; Samsher Singh v State of Punjab, 1974). (iii) Compulsory retirement of public servants. (iv) Professional misconduct - Bar Councils. (v) Licensing and cancellation (Maneka Gandhi; Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation, 1985: pavement dwellers - eviction needs fair procedure; right to livelihood part of Art 21). (vi) Demolitions: In Re: Directions in the matter of demolition of structures (13 November 2024) (the 'bulldozer justice' judgment) - Supreme Court issued pan-India guidelines: no demolition without a prior show-cause notice (at least 15 days to the owner/ occupier, served by registered post and affixed on the structure; contents - nature of unauthorised construction, details of the violation and grounds for demolition, date for personal hearing and the designated authority); a personal hearing with minutes recorded; a final reasoned order, with 15 days after the order for the owner to challenge/ remove; the order to be uploaded on a digital portal; demolition to be videographed with an inspection/ demolition report; violation of the directions is contempt and the officials are personally liable to restore the structure at their own cost and pay compensation; the directions do not apply to unauthorised structures in public places like roads, streets, footpaths, railway lines or water bodies or where a court has ordered demolition. In July 2026 the Supreme Court sent contempt petitions alleging violations of the judgment to the High Courts (verify).

sections.title: Administrative Tribunals and Quasi-Judicial Bodies
sections.summary: Arts 323A/323B, L. Chandra Kumar, tribunal independence cases and the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021.
key_points: Tribunals = adjudicatory bodies outside the regular courts, with expertise and speed. Art 323A (inserted by the 42nd Amendment 1976): Parliament may by law provide for adjudication or trial by administrative tribunals of disputes relating to recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to public services of the Union/ States/ local authorities/ corporations; Art 323B: tribunals for other matters (taxation, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, land reforms, ceiling on urban property, elections to Parliament and State Legislatures (excluded), food stuffs, rent and tenancy). Administrative Tribunals Act 1985 (Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) at the Centre; State Administrative Tribunals; some States have abolished). Other tribunals: NCLT/ NCLAT, NGT, ITAT, CESTAT, SAT, TDSAT, AFT, DRT/ DRAT, Railway Claims Tribunal, NCDRC (quasi-judicial commissions), Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, etc.

Distinction: courts (inherent jurisdiction, binding precedent, procedure under CPC) vs tribunals (statutory jurisdiction; may be bound by natural justice but not strict CPC procedure; may have technical members). Quasi-judicial bodies: authority with duty to act judicially - determination of rights after hearing (Ridge v Baldwin; Cooper). Test of quasi-judicial: the Cooper test / the 'two-fold test' - legal authority to determine questions affecting rights of subjects + duty to act judicially (R v Electricity Commissioners, 1924, Atkin LJ); Province of Bombay v Khushaldas Advani (1950) - the lis inter partes theory; Indian courts have expanded after A.K. Kraipak.

S.P. Sampath Kumar v Union of India (1987): upheld the Administrative Tribunals Act 1985 and the exclusion of HC jurisdiction on the basis that the tribunal is an effective alternative institutional mechanism; L. CHANDRA KUMAR v UNION OF INDIA (1997, 7-judge Bench): overruled Sampath Kumar to the extent that it excluded the jurisdiction of High Courts under Arts 226/ 227 and of the Supreme Court under Art 32: the power of judicial review under Arts 226/227 and 32 is part of the BASIC STRUCTURE and cannot be excluded; tribunals are competent to hear matters where the vires of statutory provisions are questioned (but not the vires of their parent statutes); tribunals act as courts of first instance; decisions of tribunals are subject to scrutiny before a Division Bench of the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the tribunal falls; direct appeal to the Supreme Court under Art 136 is retained; the Tribunal can examine constitutional validity of subordinate legislation. Union of India v R. Gandhi (Madras Bar Association case, 2010) (NCLT/ NCLAT) - the Court laid down the qualifications, tenure and independence safeguards for tribunals; Madras Bar Association v Union of India (2014, 2020 and later cases) and Rojer Mathew v South Indian Bank (2019) struck down certain provisions of the Finance Act 2017 on tribunal conditions of service; the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 abolished several appellate tribunals (including the IPAB, Film Certification Appellate Tribunal, etc.), transferred their functions to High Courts, and prescribed common qualifications/ tenure; in Madras Bar Association v Union of India (decided November 2025), the Supreme Court struck down key provisions of the 2021 Act (such as minimum age and short tenure conditions and restrictions on the search-cum-selection committees) and directed the setting up of a National Tribunals Commission (verify the current state of compliance).

Features of an independent tribunal: judicial member/ independent selection committee; security of tenure (not shorter than five years); administrative independence (nodal Ministry of Law, not the parent Ministry); appeal to the High Court/ Supreme Court. Judicial review of tribunals: by the High Court under Art 226/227 (L. Chandra Kumar); only on grounds of jurisdictional error, violation of natural justice, error of law apparent on the face of the record, perversity.

Other adjudicatory bodies: Commissions of Inquiry (Commissions of Inquiry Act 1952 - fact-finding, recommendatory; Sec 3 - Government appoints; Sec 3(4): Government must lay the report with a memorandum of action taken within six months before the House; Ram Krishna Dalmia v Justice S.R. Tendolkar (1958): a Commission of Inquiry is valid and not a discriminatory law; State of Karnataka v Union of India (1977)); statutory regulators - SEBI, TRAI, IRDAI, CCI, RBI; Lokpal; Information Commissions; National Human Rights Commission (Protection of Human Rights Act 1993). Ombudsman concept (Scandinavia - Sweden 1809; New Zealand 1962; India: Lokpal/ Lokayukta).

sections.title: Writs and Remedies against Administrative Action
sections.summary: Five prerogative writs, conditions for issuance, alternative remedy rule, locus standi and PIL.
key_points: ART 32 (Supreme Court) - a fundamental right itself; for enforcement of fundamental rights only; Art 226 (High Courts) - wider: 'for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose' (statutory/ legal rights); territorial jurisdiction (Art 226(2) - cause of action arises in whole or part). FIVE WRITS: (1) HABEAS CORPUS ('you may have the body') - against illegal detention by State or private persons; locus - next friend permitted; res judicata does not apply (Sunil Batra; Kanu Sanyal v District Magistrate, 1973: the court examines the legality of the detention at the time of the return); (2) MANDAMUS ('we command') - to compel performance of a public duty (statutory duty): conditions - a legal right to the performance, a public duty, demand and refusal; not issued against the President/ Governor personally (Art 361), against private individuals (except to perform public duty), to compel discretionary acts (unless abuse), or to enforce purely contractual duties (Sohan Lal v Union of India (1957)); (3) PROHIBITION - against inferior courts/ tribunals acting without or in excess of jurisdiction, issued before the decision is made (to stop proceedings); (4) CERTIORARI ('to be certified') - to quash orders already made by inferior courts/ tribunals/ authorities exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions for want or excess of jurisdiction, violating natural justice or error of law apparent on the face of the record (Hari Vishnu Kamath v Syed Ahmad Ishaque, 1955: the grounds; Syed Yakoob v K.S. Radhakrishnan, 1964: certiorari corrects errors of jurisdiction, not mere errors of fact or law that are not apparent; T.C. Basappa v T. Nagappa, 1954: certiorari against a tribunal; Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar v State of Maharashtra, 1966: certiorari doesn't lie against a High Court's judicial order); (5) QUO WARRANTO ('by what authority') - to challenge usurpation of a public office; conditions: the office must be public, created by statute or Constitution, substantive; the holder must have been appointed contrary to law (University of Mysore v C.D. Govinda Rao, 1964; any person may file as the remedy is not a personal remedy; Kumar Padma Prasad v Union of India (1992): the appointment of a judge without qualifications invalid). Also: Art 226 can issue 'directions, orders' - broad (e.g., continuing mandamus).

SCOPE: Writs against 'State' and 'any person or authority' performing public functions (Andi Mukta, Binny Ltd v V. Sadasivan (2005): the public law element). Not available against private contracts unless a public law element; not generally against private schools/ cooperative societies, unless discharging public functions (Federal Bank v Sagar Thomas, 2003; K. Krishnamacharyulu v Sri Venkateswara Hindu College, 1997). Writ of mandamus cannot enforce an order made by a court of law; the Court will not interfere in political questions.

CONDITIONS: (a) Locus standi - the petitioner must be a person aggrieved - the traditional rule is relaxed in public interest litigation: S.P. Gupta v Union of India (1981) (Judges' Transfer Case: any member of the public having a sufficient interest may file; PIL by letter); Bandhua Mukti Morcha v Union of India (1984); M.C. Mehta; People's Union for Democratic Rights v Union of India (1982); Dr. Subramanian Swamy; caution - Guruvayur Devaswom Managing Committee v C.K. Rajan (2003): PIL guidelines; State of Uttaranchal v Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010): guidelines to prevent abuse; PIL is not for personal gain/ publicity/ political motives ('publicity interest litigation'). (b) Alternative remedy rule: ordinarily a High Court will not entertain a writ if an effective alternative remedy exists; but the rule is one of discretion and exceptions: where fundamental rights are violated; where there's a violation of principles of natural justice; where the order is wholly without jurisdiction; where the vires of the statute is challenged (Whirlpool Corporation v Registrar of Trade Marks, Mumbai, 1998; Harbanslal Sahnia v Indian Oil Corporation, 2003; State of UP v Indian Hume Pipe Co, 1977; Union of India v State of Haryana, 2000; Commissioner of Income Tax v Chhabil Dass Agarwal, 2013: an alternative statutory remedy should be exhausted before writ in revenue matters). (c) Delay/ laches: no strict limitation, but unreasonable delay may disentitle (State of M.P. v Nandlal Jaiswal, 1986). (d) Res judicata: applies to writ petitions (Daryao v State of UP, 1961: a decision in a writ petition on merits bars a fresh petition under Art 32 on the same facts; Amalgamated Coalfields v Janapada Sabha, 1963); (e) Clean hands and suppression of material facts. (f) Writs are discretionary relief.

REMEDIES OTHER THAN WRITS: declaration, injunction (Specific Relief Act Secs 34, 38-42); damages (tort/ public law compensation); statutory appeal and revision; ordinary civil suit (Sec 9 CPC); Sec 80 CPC: notice of two months before instituting a suit against the Government or a public officer for an act done in his official capacity (Sec 80(2) allows a suit for urgent or immediate relief without notice, with leave of the court); the notice must clearly identify the claim; Bhagchand Dagadusa v Secretary of State (1927) - strict compliance; State of Andhra Pradesh v Pioneer Builders (2006): the notice requirement is mandatory but not hyper-technical; the Bar of suits (Sec 11 and Sec 9 CPC); administrative remedies - departmental appeal/ revision; and inquiries.

ART 300 and Contract: Art 299 - contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union/ State must be expressed to be made by the President/ Governor, and executed by persons authorised and in such manner as the President/ Governor may direct or authorise; a contract not complying with Art 299 is void and not enforceable against the Government (K.P. Chowdhury v State of M.P., 1967; Bhikraj Jaipuria v Union of India, 1962; Mulamchand v State of M.P., 1968: Art 299 is mandatory, but the Government's liability to restore benefits under Sec 70 Contract Act is not barred; State of West Bengal v B.K. Mondal (1962)). Government contracts are subject to Art 14 (Ramana Dayaram Shetty; Kumari Shrilekha Vidyarthi); blacklisting needs a hearing (Erusian Equipment & Chemicals v State of West Bengal, 1975; Gorkha Security Services v Government (NCT of Delhi), 2014: the show-cause notice must state the grounds for blacklisting).

PUBLIC SERVANTS: Art 309 (recruitment and conditions of service - Acts and rules), Art 310 (tenure - 'pleasure of the President/ Governor' subject to the Constitution), Art 311 (safeguards: (1) no dismissal or removal by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority; (2) no dismissal, removal or reduction in rank except after an inquiry in which he has been informed of the charges and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard; exceptions in the second proviso: (a) conviction on a criminal charge; (b) where the authority is satisfied that for some reason, to be recorded in writing, it is not reasonably practicable to hold the inquiry; (c) where the President/ Governor is satisfied that in the interest of the security of the State it is not expedient to hold the inquiry) - Union of India v Tulsiram Patel (1985); Parshotam Lal Dhingra v Union of India (1958): 'punishment' test; Moti Ram Deka v General Manager, North East Frontier Railway (1964); doctrine of pleasure; Samsher Singh v State of Punjab (1974): the President/ Governor exercises power on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. Disciplinary proceedings: principle of proportionality in punishment (Ranjit Thakur; B.C. Chaturvedi v Union of India, 1995: the court may interfere if the punishment shocks the conscience). Departmental inquiry and criminal trial can proceed simultaneously (Capt. M. Paul Anthony v Bharat Gold Mines, 1999: stay in grave cases involving complex questions of fact/ law).

sections.title: Accountability and Transparency Institutions: Lokpal, Lokayukta, CVC, RTI Act
sections.summary: Statutory accountability bodies and the Right to Information Act 2005 - timelines and exemptions are exam favourites.
key_points: LOKPAL AND LOKAYUKTAS ACT 2013 (in force 16 January 2014): Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayuktas in States (Sec 63 required States to establish Lokayuktas within 365 days of commencement). LOKPAL: a Chairperson and not more than eight members, of whom fifty per cent shall be judicial members; at least fifty per cent of members from SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women. The Chairperson: a person who is or has been the Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court or an eminent person with special knowledge of anti-corruption policy, public administration, vigilance, finance, law and management. Selection Committee: PM (Chair), Speaker of Lok Sabha, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, CJI or a Judge of the Supreme Court nominated by the CJI, and an eminent jurist nominated by the President on the recommendation of the first four. Term: five years or until 70 years of age (Chairperson/ members). Jurisdiction (Sec 14): includes the Prime Minister (except in matters relating to international relations, external and internal security, public order, atomic energy and space - and an inquiry against the PM must be held in camera and the decision is by 2/3 of full Bench of Lokpal), Ministers, MPs, Group A-D officers and officers of Central Government, officials of bodies/ boards funded by the Government, and persons receiving foreign donations above a specified amount (Rs 10 lakh per year) - the Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 offences. The limitation: no complaint after seven years from the date of the alleged offence (Sec 53). Lokpal has an Inquiry Wing and Prosecution Wing; may direct CBI. First Lokpal Chairperson: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose (March 2019). Recent: In 2025 the Lokpal assumed jurisdiction to examine complaints against a sitting High Court Judge, and the Supreme Court stayed that order (February 2025) - verify the latest position.

LOKAYUKTA (State): created by State laws (Maharashtra 1971 first). CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION (CVC): initially by executive resolution (Santhanam Committee 1964); statutory status under the Central Vigilance Commission Act 2003 following Vineet Narain v Union of India (1998) (Jain Hawala case): CBI independence, CVC to supervise CBI, directions to insulate from political influence; CVC consists of a Central Vigilance Commissioner and not more than two Vigilance Commissioners; appointed by the President on recommendation of a committee (PM, Home Minister, Leader of Opposition). CBI: Delhi Special Police Establishment Act 1946; Sec 6A (single directive requiring prior approval for inquiry against officers of Joint Secretary level and above) was struck down in Subramanian Swamy v Director, CBI (2014) as violative of Art 14; Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act 2018 introduced Sec 17A - prior approval for inquiry/ investigation into offences relating to decisions/ recommendations of a public servant (a split verdict in 2023 referred the validity to a larger Bench - verify).

RIGHT TO INFORMATION ACT 2005: Sec 2(h) 'public authority'; Sec 2(f) information; Sec 3: all citizens have right to information; Sec 4: proactive disclosure (suo motu); Sec 5: Public Information Officers (PIOs) and Assistant PIOs; Sec 6: request for information - application to PIO with the prescribed fee (Central: Rs 10), no reason need be given (Sec 6(2)); Sec 7(1): the PIO shall dispose of the request within THIRTY DAYS; where the information concerns the life or liberty of a person - within FORTY-EIGHT HOURS; transfer under Sec 6(3) - 5 days; Sec 7(5): no fee for persons below the poverty line; Sec 8: EXEMPTIONS - (a) information that would prejudicially affect sovereignty and integrity of India, security, strategic, scientific or economic interests of the State, relation with foreign State or lead to incitement of an offence; (b) information forbidden to be published by any court; (c) breach of privilege of Parliament or State Legislature; (d) commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property, the disclosure of which would harm the competitive position of a third party, unless the competent authority is satisfied that larger public interest warrants the disclosure; (e) information available to a person in his fiduciary relationship, unless larger public interest; (f) information received in confidence from a foreign government; (g) information which would endanger the life or physical safety of any person or identify the source of information given in confidence for law enforcement; (h) information which would impede the process of investigation or apprehension or prosecution of offenders; (i) cabinet papers including records of deliberations of the Council of Ministers, Secretaries and other officers (after decision, material to be made public); (j) information which relates to personal information the disclosure of which has no relationship to any public activity or interest, or which would cause unwarranted invasion of the privacy of the individual unless the PIO is satisfied that larger public interest justifies disclosure - provided that information which cannot be denied to Parliament or State Legislature shall not be denied to any person. Sec 8(2): public interest override - information may be disclosed if public interest in disclosure outweighs harm to the protected interests (even for the Official Secrets Act 1923 or exemptions); Sec 8(3): information relating to any occurrence, event or matter which has taken place, occurred or happened twenty years before the date of request shall be provided (subject to exceptions in 8(1)(a), (c), (i)); Sec 9: copyright infringement; Sec 10: severability; Sec 11: third party information; Sec 24: exemption of certain organisations (Second Schedule - intelligence and security organisations such as IB, RAW and similar agencies - but allegations of corruption and human rights violations must be disclosed (with approval of the Information Commission within 45 days for human rights; information on corruption allegations - no approval).

APPEALS AND PENALTIES: Sec 19(1): first appeal to the First Appellate Authority (an officer senior in rank to the PIO) within THIRTY DAYS from the expiry of the period within which the decision should have been made or the receipt of the decision; Sec 19(3): second appeal to the Central/ State Information Commission within NINETY DAYS; Sec 18: complaints to the Information Commission; the burden of proving that denial was justified lies on the PIO (Sec 19(5)); Sec 20: penalty - the Information Commission may impose a penalty of Rs 250 per day till the information is furnished, subject to a maximum of Rs 25,000 on the PIO for refusing to receive an application, not furnishing information within the time, malafide denial, incorrect/ incomplete/ misleading information, or destroying information; recommends disciplinary action against persistent defaulters (Sec 20(2)); Sec 22: the Act overrides inconsistent provisions of the Official Secrets Act 1923; Sec 23: bar of jurisdiction of courts (but Art 32/226 remain); Sec 12-15: constitution of the CIC (Chief Information Commissioner and not more than ten Information Commissioners) and State Information Commissions; RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 changed the term, status and salary of the Information Commissioners (made them as prescribed by the Central Government - challenged as eroding independence). Landmark: Secretary General, Supreme Court of India v Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019, Constitution Bench): Office of the Chief Justice of India is a 'public authority' under RTI; judicial independence is not compromised by disclosure; information on judges' assets and collegium decisions subject to balancing (privacy and public interest); CBSE v Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011): examinees' answer books are accessible; fiduciary exemption; Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v Central Information Commissioner (2013): personal information such as service records and assets are generally personal; Reserve Bank of India v Jayantilal N. Mistry (2015): RBI cannot withhold bank inspection reports citing fiduciary relationship - public interest; Anjali Bhardwaj v Union of India (2019): vacancies in Information Commissions must be filled in a time-bound manner.

DPDP ACT 2023 AND RTI (HOT): Sec 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 amended Sec 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act so that exemption for 'personal information' applies without the earlier public interest balancing proviso and without the qualifier that it must have 'no relationship to any public activity or interest'; the amendment was notified into force with the DPDP Rules in November 2025 (14 November 2025); challenges are pending before the Supreme Court and the debate on RTI dilution continues (verify). Digital initiatives: the Right to Services legislation in States (time-bound public services - e.g., Madhya Pradesh Lok Sewa Guarantee Act 2010), citizens' charters.
