modules.title: Intellectual Property Law (Copyright, Patents, Trade Marks, Designs, GI)

sections.title: IP Framework: Types, International Treaties, Institutions and Courts
sections.summary: Orientation questions: which statute protects what, treaty names and years, and where IP disputes are heard.
key_points: Intellectual property = creations of the mind protected by law. Indian statutes: Copyright Act 1957; Patents Act 1970; Trade Marks Act 1999; Designs Act 2000; Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999; Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act 2001; Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000; Biological Diversity Act 2002 (benefit sharing). Trade secrets/ confidential information have no dedicated statute: protected by contract and equity (common law breach of confidence).

International framework: Paris Convention (1883, industrial property; national treatment, priority right of 12 months for patents/ 6 months for designs and trade marks); Berne Convention (1886, copyright; automatic protection, no formalities; India a member since 1928); TRIPS Agreement (1995, WTO; minimum standards; India amended its laws to comply - product patents for pharmaceuticals/ agrochemicals from 1 January 2005); Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT, 1970; India acceded 1998); Madrid Protocol (international registration of trade marks; India acceded 2013); Budapest Treaty (microorganism deposit; India joined 2001); WIPO Copyright Treaty and WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (1996; India acceded 2018); Marrakesh Treaty (accessible formats for persons with print disabilities; India ratified 2014); Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health (2001) - basis for compulsory licensing flexibilities.

Institutions: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) is the nodal department; Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM, Mumbai) with offices at Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Mumbai; Copyright Office (Delhi); GI Registry (Chennai); Cell for IPR Promotion and Management (CIPAM). National IPR Policy 2016: 'Creative India; Innovative India'; seven objectives; DPIIT nodal.

Forum: IP suits are 'commercial disputes' under the Commercial Courts Act 2015, so they go to Commercial Courts/ Commercial Divisions of High Courts (specified value Rs 3 lakh). Pre-institution mediation under Sec 12A of the Commercial Courts Act is mandatory unless urgent interim relief is sought (Patil Automation v Rakheja Engineers, 2022). The Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021; its appellate and rectification functions moved to the High Courts; the Delhi High Court has a dedicated IP Division (2021). Jurisdiction for copyright and trade mark infringement suits: Sec 62(2) Copyright Act and Sec 134(2) Trade Marks Act allow filing where the plaintiff resides, carries on business or works for gain (Indian Performing Right Society v Sanjay Dalia, 2015).
key_provisions: Sec 62(2) Copyright Act; Sec 134(2) Trade Marks Act
common_traps: IPAB no longer exists (abolished 2021); appeals go to High Courts.
Product patents for pharmaceuticals in India: 1 January 2005 (Patents Amendment Act 2005).
Copyright is automatic; trade marks and patents require registration for statutory rights (unregistered marks protected by passing off).
likely_questions: Which treaty provides the minimum standards of IP protection linked to the WTO? TRIPS.
Madrid Protocol relates to: international registration of trade marks.
Appeals under IP statutes after 2021 lie to: High Court.

sections.title: Copyright Act 1957 (as amended in 2012)
sections.summary: Subject-matter, ownership, assignment, term, moral rights, fair dealing, infringement and remedies. Expect at least one question.
key_points: Sec 13: copyright subsists in (a) original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works; (b) cinematograph films; (c) sound recordings. Copyright protects EXPRESSION, not ideas (idea-expression dichotomy): R.G. Anand v Delux Films (1978) - no copyright in an idea; infringement judged by substantial similarity as seen by the average viewer/ reader. Originality: Eastern Book Company v D.B. Modak (2008) rejected the 'sweat of the brow' approach and adopted the 'modicum of creativity' standard (copyedited law reports protected for the creative input). Computer programmes and databases are 'literary works' (Sec 2(o)). Titles and short phrases are usually not protected.

Sec 14 EXCLUSIVE RIGHTS: for literary/ dramatic/ musical works - reproduction, issue of copies to the public, performance in public, communication to the public, making cinematograph films or sound recordings, translations and adaptations; computer programmes - also the right to sell or give on commercial rental. Artistic works - reproduction, publication, communication, adaptation. Films - making copy, selling/ renting, communication. Sound recordings - similar.

Sec 17 FIRST OWNER: the author is the first owner, except: (a) literary/ dramatic/ artistic works made by an author in the course of employment of a proprietor of a newspaper/ magazine - the proprietor owns for publication purposes; (b) photograph, painting, portrait, drawing or cinematograph film made for valuable consideration at the instance of another person - that person (in the absence of a contrary agreement); (c) a work made in the course of the author's employment under a CONTRACT OF SERVICE (employee) - the employer (in the absence of a contrary agreement); contrast contract FOR service (independent contractor) - author owns; (d) Government works - the Government. Cinematograph film: the producer is the author (Sec 2(d)(v)). Sec 2(d) 'author': writer, composer, artist, photographer, producer of film/ sound recording, computer-generated work - the person who causes the work to be created.

ASSIGNMENT AND LICENCE (Secs 18-19A, 30-32): Sec 18 - copyright may be assigned (including future works - the assignment takes effect when the work comes into existence). Sec 19: the assignment must be in WRITING signed by the assignor; it must identify the work, rights, duration, territorial extent and royalty; if the period is not stated, it is deemed FIVE YEARS; if territory is not stated, it is presumed to extend WITHIN INDIA; if the assignee does not exercise the rights within ONE YEAR, the assignment lapses unless otherwise specified. Sec 19(4), 19(5), 19(6). Sec 19A: dispute resolution; Sec 18 provisos (2012 amendment): authors of literary/ musical works in films cannot assign the right to receive royalties for the use of their works other than in the cinema hall (except to legal heirs/ copyright societies) - Sec 18(1) 2nd and 3rd provisos. Compulsory licences: Sec 31 (works withheld from public), Sec 31A (unpublished/ anonymous), Sec 31B (persons with disabilities), Sec 31C (cover versions - after five years of the first recording), Sec 31D (statutory licence for broadcasting of literary and musical works and sound recordings - on payment of royalty). Copyright societies: Secs 33-36 (IPRS, PPL, Novex).

TERM (Secs 22-29): literary, dramatic, musical, artistic works - lifetime of the author + SIXTY years (counted from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death); anonymous/ pseudonymous works, posthumous works, photographs, cinematograph films, sound recordings, Government works, works of public undertakings and international organisations - SIXTY years from the beginning of the calendar year following publication. Broadcast reproduction right - 25 years (Sec 37); performer's right - 50 years (Sec 38).

MORAL RIGHTS - Sec 57 (author's special rights): independently of the author's copyright and even after assignment, the author has the right to claim authorship (paternity) and to restrain or claim damages in respect of any distortion, mutilation, modification or other act in relation to the said work which is done before the expiration of the term of copyright if such distortion, mutilation or modification would be prejudicial to his honour or reputation. Amar Nath Sehgal v Union of India (2005, Delhi HC): destruction of a bronze mural amounted to violation of moral rights. Performers also have moral rights (Sec 38B, 2012).

Sec 52 FAIR DEALING AND OTHER EXCEPTIONS: not an infringement - (a) fair dealing with a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work (not a computer programme) for (i) private or personal use including research, (ii) criticism or review, (iii) reporting of current events and current affairs including the reporting of a lecture delivered in public; (aa) making of copies/ adaptation of a computer programme by a lawful possessor for backup/ lawful use; (ab) observing, studying and testing functioning for interoperability; (b)-(c) reproduction for judicial proceedings; (h) reproduction for educational purposes - use by teachers/ pupils in the course of instruction; (i) performance in the course of activities of an educational institution; (za) performance of a literary, dramatic or musical work in a religious ceremony; (zb) accessible formats for persons with disabilities (2012). The Delhi High Court in University of Oxford v Rameshwari Photocopy Services (2016, single judge; the Division Bench in 2016 remanded the matter) held that photocopying of course packs for students falls within the educational exception. Fair dealing is an open-ended standard in the common-law tradition: in the AI era, the Delhi High Court in ANI v OpenAI (2026) considered whether training generative AI on copyrighted news content is fair dealing.

INFRINGEMENT (Sec 51): doing without licence any act which is exclusive right of the owner, or permitting for profit any place to be used for communication of the work to the public, or importing infringing copies. Test of infringement: substantial copying - R.G. Anand. Secondary infringement: sale/ hire/ distribution/ import of infringing copies. CIVIL REMEDIES (Secs 55-62): injunction, damages/ account of profits, delivery up of infringing copies (Sec 58); Anton Piller and John Doe orders recognised by courts (Taj Television v Rajan Mandal, 2003; John Doe orders in sports broadcasting cases); innocent infringer is not liable for damages (Sec 55(1) proviso); suit not to be instituted in a court inferior to the District Court (Sec 62(1)). CRIMINAL REMEDIES (Secs 63-70): Sec 63 - imprisonment of not less than SIX MONTHS up to THREE YEARS and fine of Rs 50,000 to Rs 2 lakh (lesser sentence for non-profit use); Sec 63A - second and subsequent conviction: minimum one year up to three years and fine Rs 1 lakh to Rs 2 lakh; Sec 63B - knowing use of an infringing copy of a computer programme: imprisonment of not less than 7 days up to three years and fine Rs 50,000 to Rs 2 lakh; Sec 64 - police may seize infringing copies without warrant; Sec 65A-65B (2012) - protection of technological protection measures and rights management information. Registration (Secs 44-50): optional; registration is prima facie evidence (Sec 48); not a condition for protection; Registrar of Copyrights.

PERFORMERS' RIGHTS (Sec 38-39, 2012): performers' rights of 50 years; moral rights; Sec 39 exceptions. BROADCASTING: ESPN Star Sports v Global Broadcast News (2008) - live broadcast; Eastern Book Company v Navin J. Desai (2001); Super Cassettes Industries v MySpace Inc (2011; Division Bench 2016): intermediary liability under Sec 51(a)(ii) read with IT Act safe harbour (Sec 79); actual knowledge is needed; Indian Performing Right Society v Eastern India Motion Pictures Association (1977): rights of film producers vs composers; Entertainment Network (India) v Super Cassette Industries (2008): compulsory licences for FM radio/ Sec 31.

sections.title: Patents Act 1970
sections.summary: Patentability, Section 3 exclusions (3(d), 3(k)), procedure and opposition, term, compulsory licensing and remedies. Novartis and Natco are must-know cases.
key_points: Sec 2(1)(j) 'INVENTION' = a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application. Sec 2(1)(l) 'new invention' = no prior publication or use anywhere before the date of filing (novelty). Sec 2(1)(ja) 'inventive step' = a feature of an invention that involves technical advance as compared to existing knowledge or having economic significance or both and that makes the invention not obvious to a person skilled in the art. Sec 2(1)(ac) 'capable of industrial application' = capable of being made or used in an industry. Three tests: NOVELTY, INVENTIVE STEP, INDUSTRIAL APPLICABILITY.

Sec 3 - WHAT ARE NOT INVENTIONS: (a) frivolous inventions or claims contrary to well-established natural laws; (b) inventions the primary or intended use of which would be contrary to law or morality or injurious to public health; (c) mere discovery of a scientific principle or abstract theory or discovery of any living or non-living substance occurring in nature; (d) mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in the enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance, or mere discovery of any new property or new use for a known substance or mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus unless such known process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant (explanation: salts, esters, polymorphs, metabolites etc. are the same substance unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy); (e) a substance obtained by mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of properties; (f) mere arrangement or re-arrangement or duplication of known devices functioning independently; (h) a method of agriculture or horticulture; (i) any process for the medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic, therapeutic or other treatment of human beings or animals; (j) plants and animals in whole or in any part thereof other than microorganisms, including seeds, varieties and species and essentially biological processes for production or propagation; (k) a mathematical or business method or a computer programme per se or algorithms; (l) a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work or any other aesthetic creation; (m) a mere scheme or rule or method of performing mental act or method of playing game; (n) presentation of information; (o) topography of integrated circuits; (p) an invention which in effect is traditional knowledge or an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known component(s). Sec 4: inventions relating to atomic energy are not patentable.

NOVARTIS AG v UNION OF INDIA (2013, Supreme Court) - Glivec (beta-crystalline form of imatinib mesylate): patent refused under Sec 3(d); 'efficacy' in Sec 3(d) means therapeutic efficacy (for medicines); the beta crystalline form did not show enhanced therapeutic efficacy over imatinib free base; Sec 3(d) is designed to prevent 'evergreening'; the Court also held that the coverage and the disclosure requirements are distinct. COMPUTER-RELATED INVENTIONS: Sec 3(k) excludes 'computer programme per se'; Ferid Allani v Union of India (2019, Delhi HC): inventions that show a technical effect or technical contribution are patentable even if they use computer programs; Guidelines for Examination of Computer Related Inventions 2017 (Patent Office); later decisions follow the technical contribution approach (e.g., Microsoft Technology Licensing v Assistant Controller, 2023).

PROCEDURE: Sec 6 - who may apply (true and first inventor, assignee, legal representative); Sec 7 - form (application with specification); Sec 8 - applicant to furnish information regarding foreign applications (Form 3); Sec 9 - provisional specification then complete specification within 12 months (priority date = filing of provisional); Sec 10 - contents of specification (title, field, description, claims; best method; sufficiency/ enablement); Sec 11 - priority dates; Sec 11A - PUBLICATION of the application after 18 months from the priority date (or earlier on request); Sec 11B - request for examination (the Patents Rules prescribe the period; the Patents (Amendment) Rules 2024 changed some timelines - verify the current period, formerly 48 months from the priority date); Sec 12 - examination by examiner; Sec 13 - search for anticipation; Sec 15 - refusal/ requirement of amendments; Sec 16 - division of applications; Sec 21 - the application is deemed abandoned if not put in order for grant within the prescribed period; Sec 25 - OPPOSITION: PRE-GRANT opposition (Sec 25(1)) by any person after publication but before grant (grounds include prior publication, prior claiming, public knowledge or use, obviousness, not an invention/ patentable under Sec 3 or 4, insufficiency, non-disclosure of foreign filing information, anticipation by traditional knowledge); POST-GRANT opposition (Sec 25(2)) by any person interested within ONE YEAR from the date of publication of the grant; Sec 43 - grant and sealing; Sec 39 - residents of India require prior written permission of the Controller to file abroad (security); Sec 146 - working statement (Form 27 - the 2024 Rules relaxed the frequency to every three years - verify).

TERM AND RIGHTS: Sec 53 - term of a patent is TWENTY YEARS from the date of filing of the application (for PCT national phase, the international filing date); renewal fees annually (Sec 53(2)); Sec 48 - rights of patentee: for a product patent - prevent third parties from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product; for a process patent - prevent use of the process and the product directly obtained; Sec 47 - Government may use patent for its own purposes; Sec 50 - co-owners; Sec 70 - surrender; Sec 64 - REVOCATION on grounds such as not patentable, prior claim, wrongful obtaining, non-disclosure, false suggestion; by the High Court on petition or in a counter-claim; Sec 66 - revocation by the Central Government in public interest. Bolar exemption: Sec 107A(a) - use for experiments/ research or for development and submission of information required under any law regulating the manufacture, use, sale or import of any product; Sec 107A(b) - importation by any person from a person duly authorised under the law to produce and sell or distribute the product (parallel importation permitted - international exhaustion).

COMPULSORY LICENCE - Sec 84: at any time after THREE YEARS from the date of grant of a patent, any person interested may apply for a compulsory licence on any of the grounds: (a) the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention have not been satisfied; (b) the patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price; (c) the patented invention is not worked in the territory of India. Sec 92 - compulsory licences in circumstances of national emergency, extreme urgency or public non-commercial use (no waiting period); Sec 92A - compulsory licence for export of medicines to countries with insufficient manufacturing capacity (Doha/ Paragraph 6). NATCO PHARMA v BAYER CORPORATION (2012): the first compulsory licence in India, granted by the Controller of Patents (March 2012) for the cancer drug Nexavar (sorafenib tosylate); upheld by the IPAB (2013) and the Bombay High Court (2014); the Supreme Court dismissed Bayer's special leave petition (December 2014). Government use: Sec 100.

INFRINGEMENT AND REMEDIES: Sec 104 - suit for infringement is instituted in a District Court having jurisdiction (not inferior); if the defendant counter-claims for revocation, the suit is transferred to the High Court; Sec 104A - burden of proof in process patent suits (the court may order the defendant to prove that his process is different where the product is new or there's a substantial likelihood that it's made by the patented process); Sec 106 - groundless threats of infringement; Sec 107 - defences (all grounds of revocation); Sec 108 - reliefs: injunction, damages or account of profits; Secs 109-110: exclusive licensee/ patentee. Standards: Bajaj Auto v TVS Motor (2009, Supreme Court) - patent suits to be decided expeditiously; interim injunction in patent cases; Roche v Cipla (2015, Delhi HC DB) - Tarceva (erlotinib): interim injunction refused; public interest and affordability; Monsanto Technology v Nuziveedu Seeds (2019, Supreme Court) - Bt cotton: the Delhi High Court Division Bench had held that the patented gene sequence was unpatentable under Sec 3(j); the Supreme Court remitted for trial and set aside the finding at the interim stage. SEPs (standard essential patents) litigation: Ericsson v Lava (Delhi HC, 2024 - damages of about Rs 244 crore for infringement, FRAND principles); Delhi High Court has also directed 'pro-tem' deposits by implementers in recent SEP cases (2025-26).

Patent of addition (Sec 54), divisional (Sec 16), convention applications (Sec 135 - priority from foreign application within 12 months), PCT national phase (Sec 138 - within 31 months from priority date), working of patents (Sec 83 - general principles: patents granted to encourage inventions and to secure that they are worked on a commercial scale in India without undue delay and not merely to enable patentees to enjoy a monopoly for the importation of the patented article), Patent Agents (Chapter XVI; Sec 126 - registered agents), Controller's decisions appealable to High Court (Sec 117A, after the abolition of IPAB). Fees: reduced for start-ups, small entities and educational institutions (Patents Rules).

sections.title: Trade Marks Act 1999 and Passing Off
sections.summary: Registrability (Secs 9, 11), infringement (Sec 29), passing off tests, well-known marks, and remedies. Cadila and Amritdhara are favourites.
key_points: Sec 2(1)(zb) TRADE MARK: a mark capable of being represented graphically and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, and may include the shape of goods, their packaging and combination of colours. 'Mark' includes a device, brand, heading, label, ticket, name, signature, word, letter, numeral, shape of goods, packaging or combination of colours. Sound marks and other non-traditional marks are registrable when they can be represented (Trade Marks Rules 2017). Service marks, certification trade marks (Sec 2(1)(e)) and collective marks (Sec 2(1)(g)) are protected. Sec 2(1)(h) 'deceptively similar': a mark so nearly resembling another as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion.

Sec 9 ABSOLUTE GROUNDS FOR REFUSAL: trade marks (a) devoid of any distinctive character; (b) which consist exclusively of marks or indications which may serve in trade to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, values, geographical origin or time of production of the goods or services (descriptive); (c) which consist exclusively of marks or indications which have become customary in the current language or in the bona fide and established practices of the trade (generic) - unless, before the date of application, it has acquired a distinctive character as a result of the use made of it or is a well-known trade mark (acquired distinctiveness/ secondary meaning). Sec 9(2): not registrable if likely to deceive the public or cause confusion; contains matter likely to hurt religious susceptibilities; scandalous or obscene; use prohibited under the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act 1950. Sec 9(3): a mark shall not be registered if it consists exclusively of the shape of goods which results from the nature of the goods themselves, or the shape of goods which is necessary to obtain a technical result, or the shape which gives substantial value to the goods.

Sec 11 RELATIVE GROUNDS: a mark shall not be registered if, because of (a) its identity with an earlier trade mark and similarity of goods/ services, or (b) its similarity to an earlier trade mark and the identity or similarity of the goods/ services, there exists a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, which includes the likelihood of association with the earlier trade mark. Sec 11(2): a mark which is identical with or similar to an earlier trade mark and is to be registered for goods/ services not similar shall not be registered if the earlier mark is a WELL-KNOWN mark in India and the use of the later mark without due cause would take unfair advantage of or be detrimental to the distinctive character or repute of the earlier mark (dilution). Sec 11(3): prior user rights (passing off/ copyright). Sec 11(6)-(9): the Registrar's factors for determining a well-known trade mark (knowledge or recognition in the relevant section of the public; duration, extent and geographical area of use; promotion; records of successful enforcement). Sec 2(1)(zg) defines 'well-known trade mark'. Sec 12: honest concurrent use. Sec 13: names of chemical elements/ INNs not registrable.

Registration: application (Sec 18) -> examination (Sec 19) -> acceptance and advertisement (Sec 20) -> opposition within FOUR months of advertisement (Sec 21) -> registration (Sec 23). Duration (Sec 25): TEN years from the date of application, renewable for successive periods of ten years (renewal within six months before expiry; a grace period of six months with a surcharge; restoration). Sec 28: rights conferred by registration - exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods/ services and to obtain relief for infringement; Sec 31: registration is prima facie evidence of validity; Sec 32: protection of registration on the ground of honest user; Sec 34: vested rights of a prior user prevail against a registered proprietor (continuous prior use); Sec 38: assignment and transmission; Sec 45-46: registered users; Sec 47: REMOVAL for non-use - the mark is liable to be removed if it was registered without bona fide intention to use and not used, or has not been used for a continuous period of FIVE years and THREE months from the date on which it was actually entered in the register (the period of five years commencing from the date of registration plus three months); Sec 57: rectification/ cancellation; Sec 59: correction.

Sec 27: no infringement action for an unregistered trade mark, but the right of action against any person for passing off is preserved (Sec 27(2)). Sec 29 INFRINGEMENT: (1) a registered trade mark is infringed by a person who, not being a registered proprietor or a permitted user, uses in the course of trade a mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to the trade mark in relation to the goods/ services in respect of which it is registered and in such manner as to render the use of the mark likely to be taken as being used as a trade mark; (2) use of a similar mark for identical/ similar goods likely to cause confusion; (4) use of an identical/ similar mark on DISSIMILAR goods where the registered mark has a REPUTATION in India and the use takes unfair advantage of or is detrimental to the distinctive character or repute (dilution); (5) use as trade name; (6) acts of use (affixing, selling, importing, advertising); (8) advertising which takes unfair advantage/ is contrary to honest practices. Sec 30: limits on the effect - use in accordance with honest practices; descriptive use; exhaustion of rights (goods put in the market by the proprietor); Sec 35: use of a person's own name/ place of business (bona fide). Sec 142: remedy for groundless threats; Sec 124: stay of infringement suit pending rectification proceedings.

PASSING OFF (common law tort protecting goodwill): the 'classical trinity' - (1) GOODWILL or reputation attached to the goods or services; (2) MISREPRESENTATION by the defendant (intentional or not) leading or likely to lead the public to believe that the goods/ services are those of the plaintiff; (3) DAMAGE or likelihood of damage to the plaintiff (Reckitt & Colman v Borden, 'Jif Lemon' case; accepted in India - Laxmikant V. Patel v Chetanbhat Shah, 2002). Passing off applies to unregistered marks, trade dress, get-up, domain names (Satyam Infoway v Sifynet Solutions, 2004: domain names are protected as trade marks/ passing off), personality/ celebrity names (Titan Industries v Ramkumar Jewellers, 2012). Transborder reputation: N.R. Dongre v Whirlpool Corporation (1996); Toyota Jidosha Kabushiki Kaisha v Prius Auto Industries (2018, SC - Toyota's reputation in 'Prius' did not extend into India's territory; prior user and territoriality). Prior user vs registered proprietor: S. Syed Mohideen v P. Sulochana Bai (2016) - a prior user of a mark has a better right than a subsequent registrant.

TESTS FOR DECEPTIVE SIMILARITY: (a) Amritdhara Pharmacy v Satya Deo Gupta (1963, SC): ordinary purchaser of average intelligence and imperfect recollection; overall structural and phonetic similarity ('Amritdhara' vs 'Lakshmandhara'); (b) Parle Products v J.P. & Co (1972): the overall impression, 'a man of average intelligence and imperfect recollection', not by side-by-side comparison; (c) Cadila Healthcare v Cadila Pharmaceuticals (2001, SC): factors - nature of the marks, degree of resemblance, nature of goods, similarity in nature, character and performance, class of purchasers, mode of purchase, other surrounding circumstances; a STRICTER test applies to pharmaceuticals (risk of life/ health; medicines with look-alike names 'Falcigo' and 'Falcitab'); (d) Ruston & Hornsby v Zamindara Engineering (1969): infringement vs passing off - in infringement, the question is the resemblance and the likelihood of confusion; the defendant's get-up is not a defence; in passing off, the added matter/ trade dress is relevant; (e) Kaviraj Pandit Durga Dutt Sharma v Navaratna Pharmaceutical Laboratories (1965): infringement action is statutory, passing off is common law.

REMEDIES: Sec 134 - the suit shall not be instituted in a court inferior to a District Court; jurisdiction where the plaintiff actually and voluntarily resides, carries on business or personally works for gain (Sec 134(2)); Sec 135 - relief: injunction (including Anton Piller orders, Mareva injunctions, John Doe orders, orders for discovery), damages or account of profits, delivery up of infringing labels and marks for destruction; punitive damages in egregious cases (Time Incorporated v Lokesh Srivastava, 2005). Criminal: Sec 103 - applying false trade marks/ false trade descriptions: imprisonment of not less than six months up to three years and fine of Rs 50,000 to Rs 2 lakh; Sec 104 - selling goods with false trade marks; Sec 105 - enhanced penalty on subsequent conviction; Sec 115 - cognizance and investigation by an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police; Sec 107 - falsely representing a trade mark as registered. Appeals: from the Registrar/ Controller to the High Court (after the abolition of IPAB). Madrid Protocol system: India designated; international registrations through WIPO.

sections.title: Designs Act 2000, Geographical Indications Act 1999 and Other IP Statutes
sections.summary: Shorter, definition- and number-based questions: design definition and term, GI definition and term, PPVFR rights.
key_points: DESIGNS ACT 2000 - Sec 2(d) 'design': only the features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines or colours applied to any article, whether in two dimensional or three dimensional or in both forms, by any industrial process or means, whether manual, mechanical or chemical, separate or combined, which in the finished article appeal to and are judged solely by the eye; but does not include any mode or principle of construction or anything which is in substance a mere mechanical device, and does not include any trade mark, property mark or artistic work under the Copyright Act. Registrable if NEW or ORIGINAL, not previously published or used anywhere in India or elsewhere before the filing date (priority), significantly distinguishable from known designs and not contrary to public order or morality (Secs 4, 6). Sec 11 - copyright in a registered design: TEN years from the date of registration, extendable by a further FIVE years (total fifteen). Sec 19 - cancellation on grounds including prior registration, prior publication, not a design, and so on. Sec 22 - PIRACY of a registered design: applying the design for sale to any article, importing, publishing - liable to pay to the proprietor a sum not exceeding Rs 25,000 as a contract debt for any one contravention (total not exceeding Rs 50,000 recoverable in respect of any one design) or the proprietor may sue for damages and injunction (verify the monetary caps in the bare Act). Interface with the Copyright Act: Sec 15(2) Copyright Act - copyright in a design registrable under the Designs Act but not registered ceases as soon as any article to which the design has been applied has been reproduced more than fifty times by an industrial process (Microfibres Inc v Girdhar & Co, 2006, Delhi HC - designs applied to articles: the line between copyright in artistic works and design). Dissimilarity: a design is for aesthetic features judged by the eye; a patent is for functional invention.

GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATIONS OF GOODS (REGISTRATION AND PROTECTION) ACT 1999 (in force 15 September 2003): Sec 2(1)(e) 'geographical indication' in relation to goods means an indication which identifies such goods as agricultural goods, natural goods or manufactured goods as originating, or manufactured in the territory of a country, or a region or locality in that territory, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and in case where such goods are manufactured goods one of the activities of either the production or of processing or preparation of the goods concerned takes place in such territory, region or locality. Registration: GI Registry, Chennai; Register in Part A (the GI) and Part B (authorised users); applicants - association of persons/ producers/ organisation/ authority established by law (not individuals); registration is for TEN years, renewable indefinitely (Sec 18); the registration of GI cannot be assigned, transmitted, licensed or pledged (Sec 24); authorised users must register (Sec 17). First GI registered: Darjeeling Tea (2004-05). Infringement (Sec 22): use of a GI by an unauthorised person which misleads the public, constitutes unfair competition, or falsely represents; penalties (Sec 39: imprisonment 6 months to 3 years and fine Rs 50,000 to Rs 2 lakh). India's GIs include Basmati rice, Kanchipuram silk, Banarasi sarees, Alphonso mango, Tirupati laddu. TRIPS Arts 22-24: additional protection for wines and spirits.

PROTECTION OF PLANT VARIETIES AND FARMERS' RIGHTS ACT 2001 (PPVFR): PPV&FR Authority (New Delhi); registrable plant varieties must be new, distinct, uniform and stable (DUS); breeder's rights - exclusive right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the variety; term - 18 years for trees and vines; 15 years for other crops (and extant varieties 15 years from notification); FARMERS' RIGHTS: farmers can save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell farm produce including seed of a protected variety (but not sell branded seed); right to reward and recognition for conservation; benefit sharing; researcher's exemption. A landmark dispute: PepsiCo India Holdings v Kavitha Kuruganti (Delhi HC 2024-25) - challenges to the registration of the potato variety FL-2027 (check status). Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000: 10 years registered layout-design protection. Biological Diversity Act 2002: Sec 6 - applicants for IPR based on biological resources from India must obtain prior approval of the National Biodiversity Authority; benefit sharing; and the Patents Act Sec 10(4)(d)/ 25 require disclosure of source and geographical origin of biological material. Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) - prevents misappropriation of Indian traditional knowledge by providing prior art to patent offices (neem, turmeric, basmati disputes).

sections.title: Recent IP Developments (2024-2026) and AI
sections.summary: Use these as current-affairs hooks. Questions will be principle-based (fair dealing, personality rights, SEPs, compulsory licences).
key_points: ANI v OPENAI (Delhi High Court, July 2026): the first substantive Indian ruling on generative AI training and copyright - the single judge declined interim relief to the news agency, indicating that at this stage training on publicly accessible content did not amount to infringement and discussing the scope of fair dealing under Sec 52; questions on outputs and storage were left for trial (reports differ; verify the order and any appeal). Expect questions on whether AI training fits Sec 52 fair dealing and on authorship of AI-generated works (Sec 2(d)(vi) 'computer-generated work' - author is the person who causes the work to be created).

PERSONALITY RIGHTS: the Delhi and Bombay High Courts have been granting injunctions (2025-26) to celebrities and public figures against deepfakes, AI-generated voice/ image cloning and unauthorised merchandising, based on passing off, privacy (Art 21) and publicity rights (Titan Industries v Ramkumar Jewellers, 2012; Anil Kapoor v Simply Life India, 2023).

SEPs AND PRO-TEM DEPOSITS: the Delhi High Court has required implementers to make pro-tem security deposits in standard-essential patent disputes (Ericsson, Nokia, Dolby, InterDigital cases); the Court recognises FRAND obligations; damages awarded in Ericsson v Lava (2024).

TRADE MARKS: the Supreme Court's recent ruling in Super Smelters v SRMB Srijan (2025-26) recognised that cessation of design protection does not prevent trade mark or passing off protection for the same shape/ get-up - verify details; Delhi High Court decisions on well-known marks, domain names and keyword advertising continue.

PATENTS: Patents (Amendment) Rules 2024 - updates to Form 27 working statements and some timelines; the Controller's guidelines on computer-related inventions; Section 3(d) continues to apply to pharmaceuticals (e.g., challenges to patents on drug formulations).

POLICY: DPIIT consultations on copyright and generative AI (licensing models for training data); National IPR Policy 2016; Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2023 amended some penal provisions of IP-related laws (verify specifics); the Riyadh Design Law Treaty (adopted November 2024) is a recent international development (verify India's position).

PROCEDURE: mandatory pre-institution mediation (Sec 12A Commercial Courts Act) - Patil Automation (2022); IP Division of the Delhi High Court; Commercial Courts Act 2015. Transfer of IPAB functions to the High Courts under the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021.
